item.title: "Abolish ICE": Protests Erupt in NYC After ICE Agents Shoot Father with 5-Year-Old Son in Car
item.description:
Protests have erupted in New York City after a federal immigration agent shot and wounded a man in the Bronx on Thursday afternoon. As masked agents reportedly posing as construction workers attempted to arrest 28-year-old Oscar Belgal, they opened fire on his car. Belgal was shot in the neck. His 5-year-old child, who was in the back seat, was physically unharmed. Belgal was taken to a local hospital, where hundreds, including our guests, Democratic congressional candidate Darializa Avila Chevalier and New York City Councilmember Carmen De La Rosa, gathered to demand his release.

“What we saw yesterday was a prime example of why [ICE] is a terror to our communities, why it should not exist,” says Avila Chevalier. She was among multiple people assaulted by officers with the NYPD unit that specializes in protest policing, known as the Strategic Response Group (SRG). Four others were arrested at Thursday evening’s protest. Avila Chevalier, who was knocked down to the ground by officers, says, “This is why we also must demand that we get rid of and disband the SRG, because this type of response should have never happened for folks who were just simply trying to protect their neighbor.”

“I personally witnessed the NYPD escalating aggressively towards our community, barricading the community in … I also witnessed NYPD helping the ICE vehicles whisk away our neighbors and come in and out of the hospital,” adds De La Rosa.

“We have become less safe with the presence of ICE, and we need to make sure that we are actually upholding the sanctuary policies of the city. There is no reason why NYPD should be collaborating this way,” says Avila Chevalier.

item.title: S. Korea conducts 1st test launch of hypersonic glide vehicle amid NK tensions
item.description: South Korea conducted its first test launch of a hypersonic glide vehicle (HGV) on Thursday, Cheong Wa Dae said, in an apparent show of force against North Korea amid heightening inter-Korean tensions following a recent border land mine blast. The test launch was carried out to verify core hypersonic technologies, such as flight trajectories and speed, as a game-changing strategic asset capable of launching surprise precision strikes against enemy targets, presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said in a written briefing to the press. President Lee Jae Myung observed the launch in person, accompanied by Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul and other officials. An HGV is a missile system that uses a booster to accelerate and ascend into the upper atmosphere before separating from the booster to glide at lower altitudes at hypersonic speeds. item.title: Korean literature needs translator autonomy to reach global readers
item.description: INCHEON — Korean literature’s growing international recognition must be matched by sustained translation funding and greater autonomy, translators said Thursday, warning that global success cannot rest on individual passion. Speaking at “Translation: Text in Transit,” an international colloquium organized by the National Museum of World Writing Systems, Debora Smith, Anton Hur and Choi Mi-kyung called for support that enables translators to discover overlooked works while defending the human judgment behind literary translation. Smith, who translated the 2016 Man Booker International Prize “The Vegetarian” by Han Kang, recalled choosing to learn Korean when its literature was barely available in British bookstores. “Now it’s a completely different story. I see Korean literature and translation everywhere,” she said. Smith and Hur emphasized that the breakthrough reflected years of work by translators across many languages, rather than a single award or author. item.title: Strike on Ukrainian public bus leaves 30 dead as blackouts worsen in Kyiv
item.description: KYIV, Ukraine — Thirty people were killed and at least 18 were injured by Russian strikes in eastern Ukraine that included an attack on a public bus, authorities said Thursday, as an intensive pre-winter wave of attacks continued and power outages worsened in the capital Kyiv. Vadym Filashkin, head of the regional military administration, said public transport in Kramatorsk and the neighboring city of Sloviansk, in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, was halted because of the sharp deterioration in security. He accused Russia of deliberately targeting civilians, adding, “In such circumstances, we have no right to risk the lives of passengers and drivers. The safety of residents of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk is above all.” The attacks follow deadly missile strikes a day earlier in the northern Ukrainian town of Pryluky, where the death toll rose to 22, including five children. Rescuers searched through the rubble of a residential building hit by a Russian missile and at least 54 people were injured. item.title: Teen knife attack kills 1, injures 2 in Polish school
item.description: WARSAW, — A 15-year-old fatally stabbed the caretaker at his former school in Poland and wounded two other adults on Thursday, a day after a similar knife attack wounded nine in a Polish high school, police said. Police arrested the boy after the attack at the John-Paul II primary school in Leszczydol-Nowiny, a small town 70 kilometres northeast of Warsaw, a police spokesperson told AFP. "The caretaker was the first person assaulted by the former student," said Katarzyna Kucharska, spokesperson for the police in the Warsaw region. "Then a teacher and the head of the school managed to overpower him, even though he struck them with his weapon." The caretaker, 37, died of their wounds, regional police said on X (formerly Twitter). Police said they had also detained a 17-year-old boy in another Polish town after he made it known that he intended to do "something spectacular" at his school. Officers found a bag containing two knives in his apartment. Thursday's attack came a day after a 19-year-old was arrested after nine people were wounded at a high school in Ostroleka, 120 kilometres north

item.title: Tesla Korea's 'unverified' FSD under scrutiny
item.description: Tesla Korea’s vehicles equipped with supervised Full Self-Driving (FSD) will be facing tighter scrutiny after the company came under criticism during the National Assembly’s annual audit, Thursday, over the system’s lack of an official safety evaluation by relevant authorities in Korea. Some 45,000 U.S.-made Tesla vehicles equipped with FSD are currently on Korean roads, but the autonomous driving system has not undergone a government safety test. During the audit, Tesla Korea Country Manager Seo Young-deuk said the company plans to seek formal approval for FSD in Korea. He acknowledged that it has not officially requested testing by the Ministry of Land, Infrastructure and Transport or the Korea Transportation Safety Authority — two key authorities related with auto safety certification. “We have not requested any tests from the authorities,” Seo said. “If the government establishes a system and channel for verification, we will actively undergo the evaluation.” U.S.-made Tesla vehicles can currently operate with supervised FSD in Korea. item.title: Canadian poet Anne Carson wins Nobel Prize in literature
item.description: STOCKHOLM — The Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded on Thursday to Canadian poet Anne Carson, an essayist and classicist who brings a modern twist to mysticism and antiquity in her writings about love, desire and despair. The 76-year-old — who announced in 2024 that she has Parkinson's disease — was honoured "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature," the Swedish Academy said. The permanent secretary of the Academy, Ingrid Carlberg, said she had briefly spoken to Carson. "We didn't have so much time to speak. All she had time to tell me was that she is for the moment in Iceland, where she's listening to the wind." "She was taken by surprise, but very happy. I could hear that in her voice." A professor of classics with a background in dead languages, literature, anthropology and history, she was described by The New York Times in 2001 as "one of the great pasticheurs." Her unique contemporary poetry earned her several key literary prizes in the 1990s, including the 1996 Lannan Award a

item.title: China has no need or intention to weaken yuan for trade edge, central bank says
item.description: BEIJING — China has no need or intention to use yuan depreciation for a trade competitive advantage and has never engaged in competitive currency devaluation, the central bank said, rejecting criticisms from western trading partners including the EU. The central bank remarks push back against claims that China keeps its currency undervalued to make its exports cheaper and imported goods pricier, and were issued as the EU's trade chief Maros Sefcovic was in Beijing to discuss narrowing the bloc's trade deficit with China. China's yuan has strengthened about 4 percent against the U.S. dollar so far this year, defying the drag from a widening yield gap between US and Chinese government bonds. In a June speech, European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde urged global leaders to discuss undervaluation of the Chinese currency as a facet of the imbalances endangering the global economy. The bloc is concerned about its trade imbalance with China, which reached €360.6 billion in 2025, according to EU data, up 15 percent from the previous year. China lets the market play a decisive role

item.title: 'Bedford Park' director tells Korean American story she wanted to see
item.description: BUSAN — Stephanie Ahn, director of the American drama film "Bedford Park," said Thursday her longing to see a film that deeply explores the Korean American experience inspired her to make her first feature. The film, which won the U.S. Dramatic Special Jury Award for Debut Feature at Sundance, portrays an unlikely bond between Korean American physical therapist Audrey (Moon Choi) and Eli (Son Suk-ku), a Korean immigrant who was adopted by a white family. "There are so many Korean American or Asian American stories that have been made that I so admire, and they have certainly opened doors for me as well, but I felt they touched upon the Korean or Asian American experience in sort of a surface level," Ahn told reporters in a group interview held on the occasion of the Busan International Film Festival (BIFF). "There wasn't a story that reached that made me feel like I was seen personally deep inside," she said. item.title: Coupang files lawsuits against 620 bil. won fine over data leak
item.description: E-commerce firm Coupang Corp. has filed lawsuits against 620 billion won ($462 million) in fines levied by a state-run data protection agency over its massive data leak, sources said Thursday. According to the sources, Coupang has filed two separate suits with the Seoul Administrative Court seeking to nullify the fines imposed by the Personal Information Protection Commission in June this year. The Commission fined Coupang a record 624.7 billion won over privacy violations, including a massive data breach that affected more than 37 million users. The amount breaks down to a record fine of 423.6 billion won for the data breach and levies an additional 201.1 billion-won fine for the unauthorized collection of records of online user activities and other violations. It marked the largest fine ever imposed by the regulator on a single company, according to the commission. The punitive measures came more than six months after Coupang belatedly reported a large-scale data breach last November of personal information of users in Korea, including their names, phone numbers and delivery details. item.description: Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine — one of the options it had been considering as a protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POW) to South Korea. item.title: Seoul to turn Jamsu Bridge into 1st pedestrian-only Han River bridge
item.description: Seoul will begin turning Jamsu Bridge into its first pedestrian-only Han River bridge, ending vehicle traffic on the 50-year-old crossing later this month and creating new spaces for walking, resting and cultural events. Vehicle traffic will be banned from 12 a.m. on Oct. 26, after this year’s final car-free festival on the bridge, while pedestrians and cyclists will continue to use Jamsu Bridge during most of construction. The project is scheduled for completion in August 2027 and will add 22 viewing spaces designed to bring pedestrians closer to the Han River and surrounding scenery. Two sections along shipping routes will feature transparent decks that allow visitors to look down at the river below, offering views not available from other Han River bridges. The city will also convert the northern underground passage beneath Jamsu Bridge into pedestrian space, improving connections between Itaewon, Yongsan Park and the Han River. item.title: Why is imprisoned ex-official 'very angry' with Lee over lack of parole?
item.description: Lee Hwa-young, a former vice governor of Gyeonggi Province who is serving a prison sentence of seven years and eight months in connection with Ssangbangwool Group's illegal remittances to North Korea, is seeking parole from President Lee Jae Myung, with his lawyer expressing frustration over what he says is a lack of progress despite appeals made through multiple channels. Attorney Kim Kwang-min, who represents Lee Hwa-young, shared a media report on social media Wednesday and outlined his client's position. "Lee Hwa-young is now in his fifth year of imprisonment and is very angry with President Lee," Kim said in the interview. "We have conveyed through various channels his wish to be granted parole, but all we hear is that they are 'working on it,' while there has been no action." Kim also wrote on social media, "After concluding that the North Korea remittance case was fabricated, isn't the reality of completely abandoning someone who has been imprisoned for five years because of that very case far worse and more cruel?" item.title: Israel embassy marks Oct. 7 Hamas attack with memorial ceremony in Seoul
item.description: The Israeli Embassy in Korea held a commemorative ceremony on Wednesday in Seoul to honor the victims of the Hamas attack on Oct. 7, 2023, and to express solidarity and condolences to the survivors and bereaved families. The ceremony was attended by members of the diplomatic corps, Korean dignitaries, members of the Jewish and Israeli communities in Korea, and guests. It opened with a short film, followed by opening remarks, a candle-lighting ceremony, a moment of silence and Jewish memorial prayers. Video testimonies from victims and survivors were also shown. Yun Young-ki, deputy director-general for African and Middle Eastern affairs at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, took part in the candle-lighting ceremony. item.title: Gov't 'undecided' on plan to raise admission fees to royal palaces, tombs
item.description: The heritage authority said Thursday it has yet to decide whether to raise admission fees for its major palaces and royal tombs, with the planned increase still under review. The Korea Heritage Service (KHS) had planned to announce the fee hikes in November so they could take effect in January 2027, citing the relatively low fees compared with those at major heritage sites abroad. But the service said the timing of the fee increases remains "undecided," in a document submitted to Rep. Choi Min-hee for an annual parliamentary audit. In the document, the service's Royal Palaces and Tombs Center said it will instead improve visitor services in January after reviewing the free admission programs for visitors wearing hanbok and the potential financial burden of the fee hike on the public. "At present, there are not enough rest areas, information desks and facilities for people with disabilities, and the reservation systems are not sufficiently equipped," Huh Min, chief of the KHS, said. item.title: Bus, taxi workers feel vulnerable over self-driving future
item.description: Seoul’s push to expand the use of autonomous buses and taxis is raising questions about the future of transport workers, with unionized drivers calling for stronger safeguards and a greater say in a transition that could eventually threaten their jobs. While city officials say the technology will initially help address driver shortages rather than displace workers, union representatives want clear answers about their future job security, passenger safety and responsibility in the event of an accident. “Self-driving technology should be limited to supporting human drivers, instead of replacing them,” a Seoul bus union official surnamed Yoo told The Korea Times recently. “Operating without humans is neither feasible nor desirable.” He said drivers’ responsibilities extend beyond simply steering and braking to responding to passenger inquiries, preventing door-related injuries and handling unexpected incidents. item.title: 'The Assassin(s)' controversy divides viewers at Busan film festival
item.description: BUSAN — Amid escalating controversy over the film "The Assassin(s)," visitors at the 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) are far from united in their views. Among those aware of the dispute, opinions were split between discomfort and support for creative freedom. The film dramatizes the 1974 assasination attempt on then-President Park Chung-hee, which led to the fatal shooting of then-first lady Yuk Young-soo. Conservative political circles and civic groups accuse it of misrepresenting history, and a defamation complaint against the filmmakers has led to police investigations. The dispute has reached the festival itself. Cast and crew canceled their attendance at BIFF, citing safety concerns, while the culture ministry and the film community called for a strict response to threats against them. Actors Yoo Hae-jin and Lee Min-ho skipped the opening ceremony, and an outdoor stage greeting and a talk program were canceled. item.title: Recent electronic tracker damage case raises concerns over sex offender monitoring
item.description: While more than 5,000 sexual offenders are set to be released over three years starting next year, concerns are rising over a shortage of dedicated staff for post-release monitoring. The electronic monitoring system meant to prevent repeat crimes is under strain as each staffer’s workload has grown and violations and reoffenses have continued, raising questions about its ability to cope. According to indictments and court rulings submitted by the Ministry of Justice and the Supreme Court to Rep. Kim Dong-ah of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK), Wednesday, Cho Doo-soon, who raped an 8-year-old girl in 2008, damaged the external antenna of a home monitoring device at his residence in Ansan, Gyeonggi Province, in June last year. Cho was sentenced to 12 years in prison and released in 2020. He has since been under intensive 24-hour location monitoring. According to the ruling, Cho smashed the antenna under the delusion that it was beaming radio waves into his brain. item.title: Korean won rises against US dollar
item.description: The Korean won rose against the U.S. dollar Thursday, extending its gains for the fifth consecutive session. The won was quoted at 1,338.5 won per dollar at 3:30 p.m., up 1.9 won from the close of the previous stock trading session. At one point in morning trading, the won advanced to a high of 1,336.3 per dollar, marking the strongest level since Sept. 10. The won's gain came amid the broad strength of the U.S. dollar, with minutes released overnight showing that the U.S. Federal Reserve policymakers signaled inflation risks. Foreigners sold about 2 trillion won ($1.5 billion) worth of local shares during the latest regular trading session, with the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index slumping 2.62 percent to close at 6,625.93.

item.title: Record profits fail to impress Samsung investors
item.description: Even quarterly operating profit exceeding 100 trillion won ($74.65 billion) wasn't enough to impress investors in Samsung Electronics, whose shares have fallen about 30 percent from their June 19 peak. On Thursday, the Korean chipmaker estimated third-quarter operating profit at 107.4 trillion won, an increase of 782.5 percent from a year earlier and its fourth consecutive quarter of record earnings. No company, not even tech giants like Apple or Nvidia, has ever surpassed 100 trillion won in quarterly operating profit. Yet the blockbuster results did little to dispel investor skepticism over the sustainability of its earnings growth. On Thursday, Samsung shares closed at 262,000 won, down 2.42 percent from the previous session. Foreign and institutional investors sold a net 348.5 billion won and 647.7 billion won worth of shares, respectively, while retail investors bought a net 959.7 billion won. item.title: Religious cult, leader ordered to pay $277,000 in damages to victims of sexual assault
item.description: DAEJEON — A court on Thursday ordered a religious cult, its leader and No. 2 official to pay about 370 million won ($277,000) in damages to three female followers who were sexually assaulted by the leader. Jeong Myung-seok, the leader of Jesus Morning Star (JMS) church, has been serving a 17-year prison term for sexually assaulting the three women between 2018 and 2021. The victims — a Hong Kong national named Maple, an Australian named Amy and an unnamed Korean follower — sued Jeong, the church and its No. 2 official for damages. In its ruling, the Daejeon District Court ordered Jeong and the church to pay 250 million won plus interest to Maple, 80 million won plus interest to Amy and 40 million won plus interest to the Korean victim. Of the total owed to Maple, the No. 2 official, Kim Ji-seon, was ordered to pay 30 million won plus all of the interest.

item.title: Lee orders Korea not apply for CPTPP membership this year
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung ordered the government Thursday not to apply for membership to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) this year to allow time for sufficient discussions with farmers and fishermen, his spokesperson said. The government has been reviewing whether to join the major Indo-Pacific trade agreement comprising 12 countries, including Japan, Mexico, Australia, Canada and Vietnam. Together, the member countries accounted for about 15.2 percent of global trade in 2019. The move has faced opposition from farming and fishing industries, however, over concerns larger imports of cheaper agricultural and fishery products could erode their income and production bases. "President Lee Jae Myung ordered that we not apply for CPTPP membership within the year," Kang Yu-jung said in a written press briefing. "He also urged relevant ministries to listen sincerely to the voices of farmers and fishermen and continue to have discussions, rather than setting a deadline." item.title: Hanmi Pharm's obesity treatment Eppe wins domestic approval
item.description: The Ministry of Food and Drug Safety on Thursday approved Hanmi Pharmaceutical's Eppe, Korea's first domestically developed glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-based obesity treatment. Eppe is the 45th novel drug developed in Korea and the country's first domestically developed GLP-1-based obesity drug. It has been approved in five doses: 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10 milligrams. According to the ministry, the injectable drug is intended for chronic weight management in adults with obesity or for those who are overweight and do not have diabetes, as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and exercise. The drug was initially licensed out to global pharmaceutical company Sanofi in 2015 as a diabetes treatment, but the rights were returned in 2020. Hanmi Pharm then decided to develop the drug as its own obesity treatment. Eppe was initially expected to become Korea's 44th domestically developed new drug, but became the 45th after an eye treatment jointly developed by Aju Pharm and GL Pharm Tech received approval on Sept. 8. item.title: Foreign envoys discover Sejong's appeal beyond Korea's administrative capital
item.description: SEJONG — For those accustomed to Seoul’s density, Sejong, the nation's administrative capital approximately 130 kilometers south of Seoul, offers an unfamiliar Korean cityscape: cyclists follow streams to work and visitors from across the country stroll through the giant rooftop garden atop Government Complex Sejong or along wide boulevards with no utility poles or curbside parking. Founded in 2012 as Korea’s administrative city, Sejong has grown into a community of roughly 400,000 residents, shaped in large part by the civil servants and their families who moved south as ministries were relocated from Seoul. Thirteen officials from 12 foreign missions in Korea joined a two-day tour of Sejong on Sept. 29 and 30, arranged by the Sejong Culture and Tourism Foundation to introduce the planned city’s tourism assets. Kenyan Ambassador Emmy Kipsoi, one of the participants, said the visit exceeded her expectations of the city as a strictly functional government hub. “Before the visit, I knew Sejong mainly as Korea’s administrative capital, the home of government ministries and a cit

item.title: Seoul shares down for 3rd day amid inflation worries
item.description: Seoul shares closed lower Thursday to extend their losses for a third consecutive session, as elevated oil prices stoked inflation worries. The Korean won rose against the U.S. dollar. After opening 0.07 percent higher, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) turned lower to close down 177.97 points, or 2.62 percent, at 6,625.93. This comes as the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.66 percent overnight, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite declined 0.22 percent. Institutions and foreigners sold a net 1.67 trillion won ($1.24 billion) and 1.99 trillion won worth of stocks, respectively, while individuals bought a net 2.9 billion won. Investors seemed wary as higher oil prices are adding to inflationary pressures, and the U.S. Federal Reserve has signaled it may need to raise rates this year to tame inflation. In Seoul, tech stocks led the decline. Market behemoth Samsung Electronics fell 2.42 percent to 262,000 won, and its chipmaking rival SK hynix declined 2.44 percent to 1.68 million won. item.title: Korea, Egypt launch CEPA talks, upgrade ties to strategic partnership
item.description: The leaders of Korea and Egypt agreed Thursday to launch negotiations on a Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) to expand trade and investment. President Lee Jae Myung and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi also agreed to elevate bilateral ties to a strategic partnership, laying the groundwork for closer cooperation in defense, energy and technology alongside trade and investment. The agreements were announced after a summit at Cheong Wa Dae in Seoul during the Egyptian leader’s state visit. CEPA is a type of free trade agreement that promotes broader economic cooperation beyond market liberalization, including investment and other areas of economic collaboration. The talks follow an agreement to pursue the pact reached at the leaders’ previous summit in Egypt in November 2025. Their reunion in Seoul comes about 11 months later, with El-Sisi making his first visit to Korea in a decade. “I hope the CEPA talks will establish a solid institutional foundation for realizing both countries’ economic development goals,” Lee said, noting that the two countries could b

item.title: Controversy resurfaces over SK hynix's potential Solidigm IPO
item.description: Controversy has resurfaced over SK hynix’s reported efforts to list its NAND flash memory subsidiary Solidigm in the U.S., after reports said the company had selected lead managers for an initial public offering (IPO), despite repeatedly maintaining that “nothing has been confirmed.” In an effort to protect retail investors, Korean financial regulators have introduced rules that prohibit parent-subsidiary listings in the domestic market in principle while allowing exceptions under certain conditions. However, because Solidigm is seeking an overseas listing, the case has raised questions over whether SK hynix could face regulatory penalties if it fails to comply with shareholder protection requirements. Bloomberg reported Thursday that Solidigm has selected Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley as lead underwriters for its planned IPO in the U.S. next year. The offering, if pursued, is expected to raise approximately $10 billion and value the NAND flash memory maker at up to $100 billion. item.title: UNC's future plan on NK mine blast issue under wraps
item.description: The United Nations Command (UNC) is not disclosing what follow-up measures it would take in response to the North Korean land mine explosion south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL), although it recognized the North violated the 1953 Korean Armistice Agreement. According to sources familiar with the UNC, Thursday, details of possible next steps cannot be disclosed at this stage, while the absence of an immediate measure does not mean further action has been ruled out. Late last month, the UNC and South Korean military conducted a joint investigation on the site of the Sept. 21 mine blast within the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), which seriously injured several South Korean soldiers, and announced the North violated the armistice agreement by laying mines in South Korean territory. Sources said that besides the official announcement of the armistice violation, UNC so far has nothing to additionally announce, such as whether it would raise the issue to the U.N. The command’s relationship with the U.N. involves separate questions of operational authority and reporting responsibilities. UNC

item.title: Korea intensifies efforts to track hackers behind bank cyberattacks
item.description: Authorities are stepping up efforts to identify the hackers behind an unprecedented series of artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted cyberattacks targeting Korea's major financial institutions, Thursday, as a global cybersecurity firm pointed to a possible suspect based in China. CrowdStrike said in a report released the previous day that the threat actor was likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated. The firm assessed that the attacker may have been a Chinese-speaking individual, citing the use of ARTEX, a Chinese-developed autonomous penetration-testing tool and Chinese-language prompts observed during the attacks. In its report, CrowdStrike suggested that the attacker primarily used DeepSeek's V4.1-Flash as the large language model backend for ARTEX, while also using GLM-5.3 from Chinese AI company Zhipu AI and Grok 4.6 in separate Claude Code sessions. A key clue emerged from a Claude Code session in which the attacker asked the AI tool to draft a resume for a security researcher. item.description: Automobili Lamborghini Korea unveiled two of its latest high-performance models, Thursday, highlighting the country as the first Asia-Pacific market to see the Urus SE Performante and Revuelto SV. The event marked a major milestone for Lamborghini in Korea, with the brand also celebrating the delivery of its 3,000th vehicle in the country since Volkswagen Group Korea began operating the brand’s local import business. item.title: Defense companies accelerate developing systems integrating manned, unmanned weapons
item.description: Korean defense companies are advancing manned-and-unmanned teaming (MUM-T) in response to the changing nature of modern warfare. Recent wars have shown a shift toward using unmanned systems for high-risk operations, while manned systems take on command and control as well as precision strikes from the rear. Hyundai Rotem, which led the modernization of Korea’s ground forces by completing the development of the K2 tank in 2008, is developing a next-generation MUM-T tank in line with this trend. “We will expand battlefield situational awareness using various sensors and add artificial intelligence (AI) capabilities to enable AI-based command and fire control. We aim to operate the tank through cooperation with manned and unmanned systems, as well as with units at the formation level,” Kim Myeong-geun, vice president at Hyundai Rotem, said during the 2026 KorAsia Forum, Wednesday. item.title: NIS excluded from June meeting with US, Japan over N. Korean cyber threats
item.description: The National Intelligence Service (NIS) was left out of a June trilateral meeting with Washington and Tokyo on North Korean cyber threats, the agency effectively acknowledged Thursday. The exclusion belatedly came to light after a local newspaper reported that the spy agency had been barred from the fifth meeting of the Trilateral Diplomatic Working Group at the request of the U.S. side. "There had been some misunderstanding several months ago, but it is now a thing of the past," the NIS said, all but acknowledging the report. "Among states, misunderstandings can happen over different national interests. What matters is how to solve them in a timely manner," it said, adding, "There is no misunderstanding between intelligence authorities of South Korea and the U.S." "The NIS is working closely with the U.S. side on security matters such as cyber and North Korea," it said. Dave McCormick (R-PA) in Seoul, where he underscored the South Korea-U.S. alliance as the "linchpin" for maintaining peace and security in the region, and urged the U.S. Congress to continue its role as a "steadfast supporter" of the alliance, according to the ministry. item.title: The plague never went away: Cases are reported in parts of Africa and the US nearly every year
item.description: The plague, the rare bacterial infection infamously known for killing tens of millions in 14th-century Europe, never went away . It is now easily treated with antibiotics. Since the 1990s, most human cases have been reported in Africa, especially Congo and Madagascar, according to the World Health Organization . There are an average of about seven human cases per year in the U.S., according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention , mostly in rural areas of the American West. A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia recently died of pneumonia. The case has raised alarm in Russia after unconfirmed media reports suggested she might have died of pneumonic plague. Russian authorities say testing showed no evidence of plague, but the research institute has been quarantined. “People think the plague is gone, it was something that occurred 500 years ago. It’s not. item.title: Korean filmmakers urge politicians to let audiences judge amid 'The Assassin(s)' row
item.description: BUSAN — Renowned Korean directors and film industry officials on Thursday called for an end to attempts to politicize the historical film "The Assassin(s)" amid a controversy over its historical inaccuracies. Some 20 people, including directors Chung Ji-young and Lee Myung-se, made the call at a press conference in the southeastern city of Busan where the Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) is under way. "We are concerned over the situation in which evaluation of the movie is expanding into a tool for political feuds," they said in a statement. "Audiences, not politicians, should judge." They expressed concerns over presuming the intention of a film without thoroughly watching it and holding directors, actors and production companies accountable, saying such an attitude could hinder creative freedom. Thursday's press conference came a day after the Singapore International Film Festival (SGIFF) said its plan to screen "The Assassin(s)" at the upcoming film fest remains unchanged. item.title: SCIA chief nominee vows to end 'politicization' of investigations
item.description: The nominee to lead the newly launched Serious Crime Investigation Agency (SCIA) pledged Thursday to end the "politicization" of investigations and to maintain their independence. The SCIA launched last Friday as part of a major overhaul of the criminal justice system that strips prosecutors of their power to conduct direct investigations amid criticism that they had pursued political probes. "(I) will first put an end to the politicization of investigations," Kim Ji-yong told reporters. "The prosecution in the past conducted targeted, dirt-digging probes with political purposes, leading to numerous harms. "(I) painfully recognize the current situation that has ultimately led to the dismantling of the prosecution." The former prosecutor said he would make efforts to ensure the new agency "firmly" protects political neutrality and the independence of investigations. Kim is scheduled to undergo his parliamentary confirmation hearing next Wednesday. item.title: Gruesome injuries throw spotlight on France's policing of high school protests
item.description: PARIS — The police tear gas grenade shattered the 14-year-old’s jaw and many of his teeth. The officer who fired it was taken into custody a week later and charged with violent mutilation, punishable by up to 15 years in prison. Following surgery, the boy cannot speak and can only eat with a straw, his mother says. Other adolescents have also suffered life-changing injuries blamed on police weaponry during nationwide protests by high school students demanding more funding for run-down schools. In the former mining town of Lens, a 15-year-old lost a hand in an incident involving a police stun grenade. In Tours, in the wine-making Loire region, the prosecutor there says a police riot-control round is suspected in the partial blinding of a 16-year-old. Beyond physical wounds, the massive use of police arrests and tactics that government critics and human rights campaigners allege have been unnecessarily violent is giving a generation of French schoolchildren — and soon-to-be voters — a real-life education about state power and their rights as citizens, and how the two sometimes cl

item.title: Top court upholds HSBC's acquittal in short-selling case
item.description: The Supreme Court on Thursday upheld a lower court's acquittal of HSBC's Hong Kong unit on charges related to violating Korea's short-selling rules. Prosecutors earlier indicted the bank in March 2024 for violating the Capital Markets Act, which bans naked short selling, marking the first criminal case of its kind in the country. Naked short selling refers to short selling stocks without first securing them or ensuring they can be secured. Prosecutors alleged three bank employees knowingly engaged in illegal naked short selling of shares of nine publicly traded companies worth about 15.8 billion won ($11.8 million) from August to December 2021. In the first-instance trial, the Seoul Southern District Court acquitted the bank, ruling the employees' alleged offenses were not proven. The court said the employees were likely unaware of the details of the trade since the short-sale orders were placed automatically through the bank's system and they only borrowed shares after trades to cover shortfalls. An appellate court upheld the acquittal before it was finalized by the top court.

item.title: Korea's forgotten fortune: $1.1 bil. in shares left unclaimed
item.description: Nearly 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) worth of shares held by the Korea Securities Depository (KSD) remain unclaimed by some 26,000 shareholders, data showed Thursday. According to data released by Rep. Han Min-soo of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea, the KSD held 800.84 million unclaimed shares worth a combined 1.47 trillion won as of the end of August. Unclaimed shares typically arise when shareholders fail to claim shares issued through rights offerings, bonus issues or stock dividends. Shareholders may be unaware of the newly issued shares or miss notifications after changing their addresses. In such cases, the shares are held by the KSD or other designated transfer agents until their rightful owners claim them. The value of unclaimed shares rose by about 26.4 billion won in the first eight months of this year, from 1.44 trillion won at the end of last year, when 763.54 million shares remained unclaimed. item.title: Boy group ATEEZ to drop new EP next month
item.description: K-pop boy group ATEEZ will release its 15th EP, "Golden Hour: Part. 6," next month, its label, KQ Entertainment, announced Thursday. The upcoming album, set for release Nov. 13, marks the act's first release in five months, following its 14th EP, "Golden Hour: Part. 5," which dropped in June. The previous EP became the eight-piece group's third album to debut atop the U.S. Billboard 200 chart. Its lead track, "Bad," also continued a long run on major song charts, topping a local K-pop charting TV program for two consecutive weeks in September, about three months after its release.

item.title: JCS chief describes DMZ mine blast as 'provocation'; vows to review response measures
item.description: South Korea's top military commander said Thursday he had not thought of the recent mine blast near the inter-Korean border as anything other than a "provocation" by North Korea, while vowing to review response measures. Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) Chairman Gen. Jin Yong-sung made the remarks as some opposition lawmakers have raised issues with the South Korean military for allegedly refraining from depicting the Sept. 21 blast as a "provocation" by the North. "There was not a single moment when I thought it was anything other than a provocation when one of my men was seriously injured," Jin said during a parliamentary audit. "But I had not paid close attention to the fact that the term 'provocation' was not included in the announcement," he said when asked why the military had left out the term during Monday's briefing. The JCS concluded its joint investigation with the U.N. Command into the mine blast on Monday, confirming its preliminary findings that resin antipersonnel mines deliberately planted by Pyongyang south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) were the cause of the blast. item.title: FSC chief says launch of single-stock leveraged ETFs reflected various views
item.description: The chief of Korea's financial regulator said Thursday the decision to launch single-stock leveraged exchange-traded funds (ETFs) reflected various views, denying allegations it followed instructions from the presidential office. Financial Services Commission (FSC) Chairman Lee Eog-weon made the remarks during a parliamentary audit at the National Assembly in response to an opposition lawmaker's question about the reasons behind the launch. "We have listened to various opinions," Lee said during the audit. In May, 16 single-stock leveraged ETFs were listed on the main bourse, which led to extreme volatility on the market. Korea later raised the minimum cash deposit required to invest in single-stock leveraged ETFs to 30 million won ($22,400) from 10 million won in late July to curb volatility. "There had been calls (to introduce single-stock leveraged ETFs) as they are allowed overseas but not in Korea," Lee said. item.title: Seoul light festival draws 300,000 visitors to Nodeul Island
item.description: A glowing laser-and-art spectacle on Nodeul Island has drawn nearly 300,000 visitors in its first week alone, turning an island in the middle of Seoul’s Han River into one of Asia’s most captivating nighttime destinations this autumn. The Seoul Metropolitan Government said Thursday that about 299,000 people attended from the opening through Monday, as families, couples and international visitors gathered for light installations along the Han River. Now in its fourth year, the festival runs through Oct. 11, combining media art with the island’s riverside landscape and offering performances, exhibitions and interactive programs. Among its featured works is “Firmamento” by Italian artist duo Quiet Ensemble, which is being presented in Asia for the first time and uses lasers projected onto a 30-meter-by-10-meter structure to evoke a field of stars. Taiwanese artist AKA Chang presents “Multimmersion” and “PAMUN” on barges along the river, incorporating water and wind into installations designed to create moments of quiet observation. item.title: Han River venues offer Hangeul Day events, concerts in October
item.description: To mark the arrival of the crisp autumn weather and Hangeul Day, the Seoul Metropolitan Government is rolling out a month of night-lit celebrations, live acoustic sets and outdoor activities along the Han River. Beginning Friday, the seasonal program will center around two signature riverfront venues: Hangang PlayPlace at Ttukseom Hangang Park and Gwangjin Bridge 8th Avenue, an observation deck suspended directly beneath a bridge over the water. The festivities launch on Hangang PlayPlace with a tribute to Hangeul Day, a holiday celebrating the creation of the Korean alphabet. Starting at 1 p.m., the complex will morph into an interactive Hangeul Playground. Visitors can join scavenger hunts for hidden letters, paint traditional magnet sets or craft mother-of-pearl bookmarked name tags. A riverfront reading lounge stocked with books on Korean culture will offer a quiet retreat, while the venue’s third floor will host back-to-back screenings of classic Korean films, including the iconic war drama "TaeGukGi." The celebration extends late into the night. Following the daytime festivities

item.title: Seoul designs new bilingual guide for Hanoi heritage site
item.description: Visitors to Hanoi’s historic Imperial Citadel of Thang Long can now explore the UNESCO World Heritage Site with a new Korean-Vietnamese guide, created by the Seoul Metropolitan Government using its official city fonts and colors. The Seoul Metropolitan Government said Thursday that it will distribute the Korean-Vietnamese guide to mark Hangeul Day on Friday and deepen cultural exchanges with Hanoi. The project comes as Seoul and Hanoi mark 30 years of their friendship-city relationship, adding a cultural dimension to ties between the two cities. The guide covers nine major historic sites and nine key artifacts, with a numbered map designed to help visitors follow a clear route through the citadel. Among the sites highlighted are Hanoi Flag Tower, Doan Mon Gate and an underground bunker, while artifacts in the permanent exhibition are arranged chronologically to illustrate the site’s history. The Imperial Citadel of Thang Long, built during Vietnam’s Ly dynasty in the 11th century, is one of Hanoi’s major historical and cultural sites and is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage site. S

item.title: Scars from Oct. 7 fuel deep divisions over Netanyahu ahead of Israeli election
item.description: JERUSALEM — As Israel gears up for its first elections since the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attack, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his opponents are putting it at the heart of their campaigns. Nearly every poster, stump speech or televised debate seems to reference the attack, which has scarred the country and remains fresh in the minds of voters. Three years on, the worst security failure in Israel’s history now threatens to end the career of its longest-serving prime minister. “October 7 is kind of a framework for the entire political discussion that is going on,” said Tamar Hermann, an expert on Israeli public opinion at the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem think tank. “All of us are post-traumatic in a way.” Netanyahu’s opponents want him to pay for the failures that led to the deadliest day in Israel’s 78-year history and plunged the country into a series of inconclusive wars. item.title: Crowdsourced data powers Korea's official autumn foliage road map
item.description: As the summer heat gives way to crisp autumn air, travelers across Korea are preparing for one of the country's most cherished seasonal rituals: chasing the transformation of fall foliage. To help nature enthusiasts time their journeys, the Korea Tourism Organization (KTO), in partnership with the Korea National Arboretum, released the official 2026 Autumn Leaves Map, offering precise peak foliage timelines and a curated list of 36 top destinations nationwide. According to this year's forecast, the northern regions — including the Seoul metropolitan area and Gangwon Province — will see peak colors beginning in late October. Further south, regions like Gyeongsang and Jeolla will hit their colorful high point between early and mid-November. What makes this year's map particularly noteworthy is the tech-forward, crowdsourced data behind the predictions. Rather than relying solely on traditional climate models, the forecasts leverage real-time observations from the National Arboretum’s Plant Phenology Project. item.description: North Korea on Thursday rejected Seoul's planned humanitarian shipment of medical supplies as "an insult" and "political provocation." Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, made the remarks in a statement carried by the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). South Korea's unification ministry has said it planned to send 1,431 medical items covering 166 categories to a hospital in Pyongyang, necessary for diagnosis, surgery and treatment, as part of a humanitarian medical support program. The ministry secured a sanctions exemption in May from the U.N. Security Council's North Korea sanctions committee. "This is an insult to our state and mutant political-motivated provocation against it and a grave encroachment upon our national law," Kim said, dismissing the move as "a noisy and ugly act" and "another farce." item.title: Seoul Museum of History extends evening hours with autumn exhibitions, performances
item.description: The Seoul Museum of History is turning autumn evenings into an invitation to linger, with exhibitions, hands-on workshops, performances and traditional market stalls running into the night. The museum has extended its evening hours through Nov. 30, keeping its permanent and special exhibition galleries, city model theater and Seoul History Archives open until 9 p.m. on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. The expanded hours, which began Sept. 15, are accompanied by programs designed to give visitors new ways to experience Seoul’s history and culture after work and on weekends. A traditional market called Seoyeokbak Jajetgeori will run Friday through Sunday, with stalls inspired by Joseon-era markets offering traditional crafts, cultural goods, food and drinks. On Friday and Saturday, the market will remain open from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m., while Sunday’s hours will run until 5 p.m. The museum will also host Exhibition Night Talk, in which curators who organized exhibitions explain their themes and introduce key artifacts directly to visitors. item.title: Veterans ministry recommends local governments raise compensation for veterans
item.description: The veterans ministry has issued guidelines advising local governments to increase their honorary allowances for veterans of the 1950-53 Korean war and the Vietnam War to help reduce discrepancies in payouts between regions, officials said Thursday. Under the guidelines, the ministry recommended that basic local governments and metropolitan governments gradually raise their monthly payments to 119,000 won ($88.97) and 109,000 won, respectively, by early 2029. The veterans ministry offers a monthly compensation of 490,000 won for veterans above the age of 70 who fought in the Korean War and the Vietnam War. Additional allowances are separately given to the war veterans by basic local governments and the metropolitan governments, but the amounts of payouts have varied significantly between regions. For instance, the southwestern cities of Jeonju and Jeongeup offer a sum of 140,000 won, the lowest among cities and provinces, whereas Hwacheon county in the eastern Gangwon Province offers the highest amount of 660,000 won each month. item.title: Hyosung Heavy Industries builds test facility for 2-gigawatt HVDC controller
item.description: Hyosung Heavy Industries, the power equipment and grid infrastructure unit of Korean conglomerate Hyosung Group, has built a facility to test the performance of its 2-gigawatt high-voltage direct current (HVDC) controller, marking a first for Korea using homegrown technology, the company said Thursday. The hardware-in-the-loop simulation system, recently installed at the company's research center in Gwacheon, Gyeonggi Province, links an actual HVDC controller to a simulated 2-gigawatt converter valve and power grid. This lets engineers check how the controller responds under conditions close to those of a real grid, the company said. HVDC technology converts alternating current into direct current to carry large amounts of electricity over long distances with less power loss. item.title: [COVER STORY] K-defense expands global footprint amid shifting security order
item.description: The global security order is undergoing one of its most profound transformations since the end of the Cold War, as the prolonged Russia-Ukraine war and Middle East conflicts push countries around the world to strengthen their own military capabilities and secure their defense supply chains. These ongoing conflicts, which experts describe as an era of global rearmament, are offering chances for Korea's defense industry to expand as a global player, while the industry also grapples with challenges such as supply chain disruptions. Experts and industry figures see three major factors accelerating the global rearmament trend, according to Kang Eun-ho, former head of the Defense Acquisition Program Administration (DAPA). The first factor is a shift in the United States' approach to international security. The U.S., which helped create the postwar international security architecture, is increasingly putting its "America First" policy in action, while calling on its allies to assume a greater share of the burden for their own defense. item.title: Seoul museum traces history of Hangeul typewriters
item.description: Long before digital touchscreens and predictive text algorithms reshaped daily communication, inventors struggled with a complex puzzle: how to fit the intricate structure of the Korean alphabet onto a mechanical keyboard. Opening Friday at the G-Valley Industrial Museum in Seoul, a new exhibition titled "The Type-Writing Machine for Hangeul" traces eight decades of mechanical innovation behind the Korean script. The timing is especially symbolic, coinciding with the centennial of both Hangeul Day and the release of the Korean Braille system. The exhibition explores the evolution from early 20th-century vertical script to modern horizontal layouts, featuring over 40 rare typewriters, archival photographs and vintage media. At the center of the collection is a newly restored replica of the 1914 Lee Won-ik typewriter, widely recognized as the earliest attempt to mechanize Korean writing. Created in the United States by modifying a Smith Premier No. 10 typewriter, the machine laid the groundwork for decades of technological experimentation. item.title: Korea's rice production projected to fall 0.6% in 2026: data ministry
item.description: SEJONG — Korea's production of rice, a key staple in the country's diet, is estimated to decline 0.6 percent in 2026 due to a reduction in cultivation area, data showed Thursday. Rice output is expected to total 3.51 million tons, down from the previous year's 3.53 million tons, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics. The projected decline comes as the area under rice cultivation fell 1.1 percent to 670,000 hectares this year from 678,000 hectares a year earlier. The reduction reflects government efforts to adjust rice production, including support for farmers switching to other crops. By region, combined production in South Jeolla Province and Gwangju is estimated to reach 738,000 tons this year, followed by South Chungcheong Province with 689,000 tons and North Jeolla Province with 533,000 tons. Although rice has traditionally been a staple food for Koreans, its consumption has steadily declined, largely due to dietary changes and a growing preference for alternatives, such as wheat-based foods. The data ministry plans to release the final figures in November.

item.title: Korea says no confirmed fuel exports to Russia, vows strict enforcement of export controls
item.description: Korea is strictly enforcing its export controls on Russia, the foreign ministry said Thursday, stressing that no exports of commercial petroleum products to Russia have been confirmed through customs clearance procedures. Currently, Korea prohibits exports of strategic items to Russia and subjects an additional 1,402 non-strategic items that could potentially be used for military purposes to case-by-case export authorization, according to the ministry. "The controlled items are determined through interagency discussions after comprehensively considering their potential military use, economic impact and international coordination," the ministry said in an explanatory note jointly issued by the industry ministry and the customs agency. Outbound shipments to Russia dropped to $4 billion in 2025 from $10 billion in 2021 as South Korea joined international efforts to maintain peace through export controls "despite the economic burden on companies and the public," the ministry noted. item.title: 181 language learners travel to Korea for Sejong Institute contest
item.description: HWASEONG, Gyeonggi Province — Amira Kamal Mohamed says she used to be a shy person who rarely spoke. That began to change a decade ago, when she took up Korean while living in her home country of Egypt. She found the language gave her far more ways to put her feelings into words than her native Arabic. "In Arabic, 'sad' is just 'sad' and 'happy' is just 'happy,' but Korean has so many different expressions," said Mohamed, who studies at the King Sejong Institutes in Cairo and hopes to become a Korean language interpreter. "It let me express my emotions much more richly." Mohamed was among 181 outstanding learners from 71 countries invited to Korea by the King Sejong Institute Foundation. On Wednesday, they gathered at Hotel Prumir in Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province, to cheer on the 20 finalists of the foundation's Korean speaking and writing contests. The event came two days before the 100th anniversary of the establishment of Hangeul Day this Friday. item.title: Korea has no plans to follow US push to replace term AI with 'super intelligence'
item.description: Korea is not considering to replace the term artificial intelligence (AI) with “super intelligence,” or SI, according to the Ministry of Science and ICT, distancing itself from a terminology push underway in the United States. An official from the ministry told The Korea Times that the government has no plans of replacing AI with SI. “There has been no consideration at our level of using such terminology,” the official said on Tuesday. The clarification came after Deputy Prime Minister and Science Minister Bae Kyung-hoon, during a National Assembly audit earlier in the day, used the term SI while describing U.S. efforts to secure leadership in advanced AI competition. The Donald Trump administration has been promoting the use of SI instead of AI. Trump signed an executive order titled "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence" on Sept. 29, requiring federal executive agencies to use SI instead of AI in official documents, including websites, reports and policy papers. item.title: How closer China-US ties and more Xi-Trump summits could work in Iran's favor
item.description: China and the US — Iran's key partner and its chief adversary — found firmer common ground on Tehran at the Washington summit last month, and further head-of-state diplomacy could work in Iran's favor, according to analysts. Iran was on the agenda when the presidents of the United States and China met in Beijing in May and again in Washington in September. There was no direct reference to Tehran in Beijing's statement after the May summit, but following the September meeting China was more specific, saying it and the U.S. agreed that Iran must uphold its commitment against developing nuclear weapons. In an eight-point consensus, the two powers also agreed that no country or organisation should impose tolls on international waterways, according to the Chinese foreign ministry. Chinese state news agency Xinhua also reported that Xi Jinping said in Washington that China hoped that the U.S. and Iran would resolve their conflict through dialogue, prompting thanks in a social media post from Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. item.title: [VIDEO] Korean fans throw parties for idols who never come. Cafe owners love it
item.description: More than 100 people filed into a small cafe in Seoul's Hongdae area on Sept. 12 to celebrate the birthday of Felix, a member of K-pop group Stray Kids. Felix was not there. No one expected him to be. The event, known in Korea as a birthday cafe, is far from rare. In Hongdae alone, nearly 100 happen every week. Not all of them are for idols. During our visit, cafes across the neighborhood were also celebrating animated characters and virtual YouTubers. For Korea's coffee shops, the trend has become a lifeline. The country had 107,055 cafes in 2024, and the number fell for the first time in early 2025 as profits came under strain. In a market that crowded, a fan event guarantees what owners struggle to buy: customers. The math The arrangement is simple. Fans rent an ordinary cafe for several days and promise the owner a minimum number of sales. Felix's organizers committed to 350 drinks over four days, at about $5.50 each. item.title: Budget minister calls for 'virtuous cycle' of spending, growth and tax revenue
item.description: Korea's budget minister on Thursday stressed the need to establish a "virtuous cycle" of proactive fiscal spending, economic growth and higher tax revenue, noting the government's proposed Future Fund could play a key role in achieving this goal. Budget Minister Park Hong-geun made the remarks during a parliamentary audit at the National Assembly, outlining the ministry's vision for pursuing proactive and effective fiscal management to lay the groundwork for growth. "We will establish a virtuous cycle in which proactive fiscal spending drives growth, which in turn generates higher tax revenue," Park said. "We will boldly overhaul spending structures to ensure the sustainability of the country's public finances," he added, describing the Future Fund as a critical tool for achieving this goal. The Future Fund, which the government plans to launch next year, will channel "windfall tax revenue" from the semiconductor boom into investments aimed at promoting sustainable economic growth. item.title: Condé Nast Traveler readers vote Seoul as world's No. 1 big city
item.description: A vibrant mix of centuries-old tradition, hypermodern technology and unstoppable pop culture has officially shifted Asia’s travel center of gravity. Seoul has taken the crown as the world's best big city. In the 2026 Readers’ Choice Awards published this week by Condé Nast Traveler, the capital of Korea dethroned Tokyo to secure the No. 1 spot for the very first time. The victory marks a dramatic surge from its fifth-place finish last year, placing Seoul ahead of established global hubs like Shanghai, Sydney, Paris and Singapore. More than 798,000 readers cast votes in this year's 39th annual survey, signaling a clear shift in how global travelers view the Asian metropolis. While the worldwide frenzy surrounding K-pop, K-dramas and skin care initially put Seoul on the bucket list for millions of travelers, voters cited the city’s complex, 2,000-year history and its balance of contrast as the real key to its enduring appeal. Within a single neighborhood, visitors can step from a neon-lit smart district straight into a quiet courtyard surrounded by traditional Korean architecture.

item.title: Assembly speaker meets Italian parliamentary leaders, Vatican officials to discuss cooperation
item.description: National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik has met with Italian parliamentary leaders and senior Vatican officials on his four-nation trip to Europe to discuss bilateral cooperation, his office said Thursday. During his meeting with Italian Chamber of Deputies President Lorenzo Fontana in Rome on Wednesday (local time), Cho discussed ways to expand people-to-people and parliamentary exchanges and step up economic and industrial cooperation. "Following the elevation of the two countries' relations to a 'special strategic partnership,' cooperation has also expanded rapidly in future industries, including artificial intelligence, semiconductors, space and defense," Cho said. Cho also invited Fontana to visit Korea next year on the occasion of the country's hosting of World Youth Day 2027. Separately, the speaker met with Gian Marco Centinaio, vice president of the Italian Senate, to discuss expanding exchanges between the countries' parliaments and strengthening economic cooperation. item.title: Nepal ends search for thousands of flood victims, leaving some families angry and others relieved
item.description: KATHMANDU, Nepal — The families of thousands of people who remain missing in Nepal weeks after catastrophic floods devastated the country have expressed mixed feelings after the government said this week that it is stopping the search for victims. The office of Prime Minister Balendra Shah decided on Monday that search and rescue operations for victims of the Aug. 26 floods will cease. Instead, authorities will concentrate on rehabilitation and reconstruction including restoring roads and bridges cut off by floods, particularly in remote areas where damaged infrastructure has made aid deliveries difficult. Rescuers have so far recovered the bodies of at least 1,455 people, but 5,285 others remain missing, including hundreds of foreigners. The government estimates reconstruction and recovery will cost $4.77 billion. Nearly 33,000 people have been affected and about 7,500 homes were damaged or destroyed. Hopes for finding survivors were briefly revived after two Nepalese workers were rescued from an underground tunnel at the Trishuli hydropower project on Sept. 4, and again two days late

item.title: I-dle's Yuqi to release self-written Chinese-language mini album '27'
item.description: At 27, pop stars are often asked to look polished, invulnerable and hyper-curated. But for Yuqi, a member of K-pop group i-dle, turning 27 is an invitation to embrace friction, vulnerability and unfiltered self-love. Marking her solo return after a little more than a year, Yuqi is releasing her second mini album "27" on Thursday. Fully written and composed by Yuqi herself, the six-track Chinese-language project uses the sunflower as a central metaphor: a bloom that holds unspoken anxieties beneath its bright face, yet persistently turns toward the sun. Prior to the full release, the prerelease track "I Like You" signaled strong international momentum, topping YouTube’s daily trending music video charts in Singapore and Hong Kong while entering charts in over half a dozen countries, including Canada and Australia. Ahead of the release, Yuqi sat down for a Q&A to discuss her personal evolution, musical experimentation and what it means to be unapologetically yourself. item.title: HYBE takes flagship Weverse Con festival overseas for 1st time with India debut
item.description: HYBE — the Korean entertainment giant behind global icons like BTS and SEVENTEEN — is bringing its flagship music showcase, Weverse Con Festival, to New Delhi on March 27 and 28 for its very first overseas edition. HYBE said Thursday that Weverse Con Festival India will be held with HYBE India, bringing together leading K-pop artists and artists from India’s music scene for a two-day event. The festival will mark the first time Weverse Con Festival has been held outside Korea since its launch in 2023. Weverse Con Festival has brought together artists across generations and genres, expanding its lineup from 20 acts in its first year to 30 acts this year. HYBE said the India edition will feature top K-pop artists alongside leading Indian musicians, with the lineup scheduled to be announced in October. The festival will also feature fan participation events and programs offering attendees opportunities to experience K-pop culture beyond live performances. HYBE said Weverse Con Festival India is designed to connect K-pop and Indian music while bringing together fan communities from both

item.title: Canada will not allow assisted suicide for those with only mental illness
item.description: MONTREAL — Canada will not allow medically assisted suicide for people whose only condition is mental illness, the justice minister said Wednesday, seeking to close debate on one of the country's most controversial healthcare issues. Canada legalized assisted dying for those at the end of life in 2016. The right was extended to those suffering from serious and incurable illnesses in 2021, even if death was not "reasonably foreseeable." Initially, Canada was to allow assisted death regardless of condition by 2024, but that date was pushed back three years, with the government saying it wanted to make sure that the already overwhelmed mental health system was ready. Without government action, people exclusively suffering from a mental illness would have had access to assisted suicide in March, when the exclusion was set to expire. But Justice Minister Sean Fraser told reporters on Wednesday that Canada's Liberal government plans to pass legislation that will prohibit assisted suicide for people whose only underlying medical condition is mental illness. item.title: New major crimes unit, police likely to face friction over unclear jurisdiction
item.description: The freshly launched agency dedicated to investigating "major crimes" may be headed for a turf war with the police due to a still unclear line between their jurisdictions, observers said Thursday. The new Serious Crime Investigation Agency (SCIA) set sail at the start of this month under a recent revision to the Criminal Procedure Act that effectively dismantled the previous prosecution system, leaving the prosecution with only the right to indict and maintain indictments against criminals. The right to investigate has been split between the SCIA and the police, with the SCIA tasked with investigating seven major crimes. The revision defines such crimes as those related to corruption, business and economy, defense procurement, narcotics, national security, cybercrimes and distortion of the law, but there still exists ambiguity, such as what constitutes a "major" crime or should the SCIA be required, if not allowed, to investigate what may be considered petty crimes if related to corruption, narcotics or any other crimes stated in the law. item.title: Chinese-speaking hacker possibly linked to AI-driven attacks on S. Korean banks: report
item.description: U.S. cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said an unidentified hacker believed to be a Chinese speaker used artificial intelligence (AI)-powered hacking tools to breach multiple Korean financial institutions and steal data. In a report released Wednesday (U.S. time), CrowdStrike said the attacker used ARTEX, an open-source AI-powered penetration-testing tool developed in China, alongside large language models (LLMs) to carry out cyberattacks between late September and early October. The findings come amid a series of data breaches at Korean financial institutions, including Hana Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and Shinhan Bank, prompting financial authorities and investigators to launch probes into the incidents. According to CrowdStrike, the compromised systems included a bank's loan inquiry service used by financial brokers and another bank's mobile work-support system for employees. "While this activity has not been attributed to a named adversary, the threat actor is likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated," CrowdStrike said in the report. item.title: Attacks on Saudi airports claimed by Houthi rebels kill 3 people, officials say
item.description: CAIRO — Two attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia claimed by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen killed three people Wednesday, Saudi officials said, as the kingdom was pulled deeper into the latest front in the Iran war. The Saudi General Authority for Civil Aviation did not blame any party for the attacks at Abha and Riyadh’s King Khalid international airports, but Houthi rebels took credit earlier for the airport strikes. The attack on Abha airport killed Moroccan and Algerian residents and wounded 28 other people, while the attack on King Khalid airport killed a Sudanese national and wounded eight other people, officials said. As Riyadh has been targeted over the past week, new cage-like fences have been erected around fuel tanks and other equipment of the Saudi state-run Aramco oil company near the capital's airport. The kingdom, the world’s top oil exporter, has seen oil and military assets targeted in recent days, posing a threat to crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where traffic has been curtailed due to the Iran war. item.title: Seoul shares extend losses late Thursday morning amid inflation worries
item.description: Seoul shares extended losses late Thursday morning, tracking Wall Street's downturn, as elevated oil prices stoked inflation concerns. After opening 0.07 percent higher, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) backtracked almost immediately, trading down 54.22 points, or 0.8 percent, to 6,749.68 as of 11:20 a.m. Overnight, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.66 percent, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite declined 0.22 percent. Institutions and foreigners sold a net 457.28 billion won ($342 million) and 666.37 billion won worth of stocks, while individuals bought a net 834.66 billion won. Overall investors seemed wary as higher oil prices are adding to inflationary pressures, and the U.S. Federal Reserve has signaled it may need to raise rates this year to tame inflation. In Seoul, large-cap stocks were mixed. Market behemoth Samsung Electronics fell 0.56 percent, and top carmaker Hyundai Motor declined 3.05 percent. item.title: Cornell gang-rape accuser was 'misled' about criminal investigation, her lawyer says
item.description: ITHACA, N.Y. — The woman accusing several men of raping her at a Cornell University fraternity party was “misled” about the status of the criminal investigation in the weeks after she went to police, her lawyer said Wednesday. Even as she took her allegations about a 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity house through Cornell's internal disciplinary process, the university's police department gave her the impression that a criminal investigation was continuing, lawyer Thomas Giuffra told The Associated Press. In fact, the criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, the local prosecutor, made the decision not to go forward with a criminal case within days of the woman giving her first substantial interviews to police. Van Houten has said that he asked Cornell's police department to convey the decision to the woman, who is referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, but never spoke personally to her or her lawyer. item.title: N. Korea rallies loyalty with celebratory events ahead of party founding anniversary
item.description: North Korea is building a festive mood and stirring public loyalty ahead of the 81st founding anniversary of the Workers' Party of Korea (WPA), with various events under way. The Union of Agricultural Workers of Korea, one of the country's four labor organizations, held its celebration Wednesday, the Rodong Sinmun reported. Participants at a debate session called for stronger party leadership and more rigorous ideological education. They also stressed the need to meet the party's grain production targets, the paper said. Art events have also taken place ahead of the Oct. 10 anniversary. A performance by the Youth Central Art Propaganda Team took place Wednesday. On the same day, party cadres and artists attended the opening ceremony of the National Art Exhibition at the Korean Central Art Gallery. The paper ran a front-page article urging readers to carry on the party's history, ideology and founding spirit. item.title: Lee set to hold summit with Egyptian president on economic cooperation
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi agreed to elevate bilateral ties and expand cooperation in trade, defense and other areas during their summit Thursday. The two leaders made the announcement in a joint press briefing following their talks at Cheong Wa Dae in Seoul, where they agreed to upgrade the bilateral relations to a strategic partnership. "Today in Seoul, we issued a joint statement elevating our bilateral relations to a strategic partnership and agreed to turn our previous agreements into tangible outcomes for the people of both countries," Lee said. The leaders also officially announced the launch of negotiations for a comprehensive economic partnership agreement (CEPA), following their agreement on the trade pact during their summit in Cairo last year. CEPA is a type of free trade agreement that promotes broader economic cooperation beyond market liberalization, including investment and other areas of economic collaboration. item.title: Korea extends current account surplus in August amid solid exports
item.description: SEJONG — Korea posted a current account surplus in August, the central bank said Thursday, the second highest on record, on the back of the robust exports amid the global semiconductor upcycle. The current account surplus totaled $46.1 billion in August, up $4 billion from a month earlier, according to data by the Bank of Korea (BOK). Compared with the same month in 2025, the figure jumped $36.2 billion. It marked the second-largest figure, following $49.73 billion set in June this year. The figure remained above the $40 billion mark for the third consecutive month. In July, it stood at $42 billion. Over the January-August period, the current account surplus totaled $279.2 billion, nearly quadrupling from the same period a year earlier. The BOK said the goods account posted a surplus of $46.81 billion in August, as exports shot up 82.1 percent on-year to $104.8 billion in the month, while imports rose 23.8 percent to $57.99 billion.
