item.title: Shinhan, Kookmin, Hana data breaches fuel concerns over AI-powered cyberattacks in financial sector
item.description: A series of data breaches at Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and Hana Bank, three of Korea’s largest commercial banks, has heightened concerns in the financial sector over increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks using artificial intelligence (AI). On Friday, KB Kookmin Bank said that personal information belonging to 119 customers was leaked after abnormal external access to a mobile system used by employees. The leaked information varied by customer and included names, phone numbers, addresses and resident registration numbers in encrypted format. "We have activated an emergency response system across the company, including a thorough review of all our processes to prevent further damage and recurrence," a Kookmin Bank official said. Later that day, Hana Bank said personal information belonging to 89 customers had been exposed following an external hacking agent’s attempt to gain unauthorized access to its sales support system. item.title: 'The Assassin(s)' actors to skip BIFF events amid controversy over historical inaccuracies
item.description: Actors who starred in "The Assassin(s)" will not attend events at the upcoming Busan International Film Festival (BIFF), the film's distributor said Friday, amid allegations over historical distortion in the Korean film. The decision comes after some critics raised concerns that the historical film, which deals with the 1974 assassination attempt on then Korean President Park Chung-hee, resulting in the death of the first lady, implies that Park or intelligence authorities were possibly behind the case. "After careful consideration, and taking into account the safety of audiences and attendees, we have decided not to participate in the BIFF's opening ceremony or the Outdoor Stage Greeting scheduled for Oct. 7," Hive Media Corp. said in an English-language statement posted on its social media account. Lead actors Yoo Hae-jin and Lee Min-ho were set to take part in the opening ceremony scheduled for Tuesday, while director Hur Jin-ho, actor Park Hae-il and the other two actors were set to participate in the outdoor event the following day to introduce the film. item.title: Defense chief highlights S. Korea-US alliance, readiness on 1st visit to USFK base
item.description: Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul underscored the South Korea-U.S. alliance and their firm combined readiness during his first visit to the main U.S. military base south of Seoul on Friday, his office said. The trip marked Kang's first visit in his new capacity to Camp Humphreys in Pyeongtaek, about 60 kilometers south of Seoul, since taking office last month. Kang, a retired Army general and former deputy commander of the South Korea-U.S. Combined Forces Command (CFC), met with U.S. Forces Korea (USFK) Commander Gen. Xavier Brunson and discussed "key pending issues," the defense ministry said, without providing further details. "Minister Kang reaffirmed the solid combined defense posture and close coordination between South Korea and the United States," the ministry said in a release. item.description: Korea and Japan are trading claims over the average prices of mobile phone plans, with a Seoul-based telecom operators’ association challenging a recent Japanese government report that ranked Seoul as the most expensive cities for mobile services. item.title: Hyundai Motor's sales slump deepens beyond strike fallout
item.description: Hyundai Motor’s push to reverse its sales decline comes under a tougher test in the fourth quarter, as its long-time rivals and emerging players show greater resilience. The carmaker sold 49,022 vehicles in Korea last month, down 25.7 percent from a year earlier. The company attributed the decline largely to fewer operating days caused by the Chuseok holiday and pent-up demand ahead of its new strategic model launches. It also pointed to the lingering effects of production disruptions from the 111-day labor dispute that ended in August. But the scale of Hyundai’s local sales decline stands out, as Kia fared much better with a sales fall of 6.7 percent during the same period. The contrast is even sharper when looking at overall performance, with Hyundai Motor reporting a sales drop of 16 percent here and abroad. The carmaker also reported an overseas sales fall of 13.9 percent. Kia’s global sales rose 5.1 percent in September from the previous year, with overseas sales increasing 7.5 percent. The automaker also posted a record third-quarter sales figure of more than 846,000 vehicles.

item.title: President Lee, first lady meet citizens at traditional market
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung and first lady Kim Hea Kyung visited a traditional market in Seoul on Friday and met with citizens in the president's latest public outreach, a presidential spokesperson said. The presidential couple toured Yeongcheon Traditional Market in Seoul following their attendance at a ceremony marking the Day of Older Persons, and heard from merchants and citizens, presidential spokesperson Kang Yu-jung said in a press release. During the visit, Lee and Kim also talked to merchants and purchased food from them before having lunch at a restaurant in the outdoor market, where they chatted with other customers, Kang said. The market visit marks the latest in a series of Lee's public outreach activities, with the president often visiting markets across the country to speak with people.

item.title: How 29 bridges built modern Seoul
item.description: Long before millions of commuters swept across the Han River daily in sleek subways and air-conditioned sedans, crossing the massive waterway dividing northern and southern Seoul was a hazardous undertaking. In the Joseon Dynasty, travelers relied on simple wooden ferryboats or temporary pontoon structures fashioned from long rows of skiffs bound together with thick rope. Today, the river is spanned by dozens of concrete and steel veins that do far more than transport traffic. They tell the story of Korea’s transformation from an impoverished, war-torn nation into a sprawling global metropolis. Seoul’s Future Hangang Project Headquarters on Friday published two new volumes in its "Hangang Story Series," a cultural and historical chronicle capturing the city's evolution through the lens of its iconic bridges. The two-volume release, titled "Bridges of the Han River," examines 29 specific bridges — 23 within Seoul proper and six bordering the capital — tracing their history from pre-industrial pontoon crossings to the hyper-engineered megastructures of the present day. The architect

item.title: Parliamentary committee passes resolution calling for expulsion of opposition lawmaker
item.description: A parliamentary committee on Friday passed a resolution led by the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) to demand the expulsion of Rep. Kim Tae-kyu over his remarks denying that former President Chun Doo-hwan had committed an "insurrection." Kim of the main opposition People Power Party (PPP) came under fire after he appeared in a YouTube interview the previous day and said he did not consider either Chun or former President Yoon Suk Yeol, who declared martial law in December 2024, to have committed insurrection. Chun was sentenced to death in 1996, later reduced to life imprisonment, on charges that included insurrection for his roles in a 1979 coup and the military's violent suppression of the Gwangju democratization movement in May 1980. In a vote at the National Assembly's House Steering Committee, the resolution passed 16-0, with PPP lawmakers refusing to take part in the vote. "Defending those who committed insurrection and undermined the constitutional order amounts to giving up one's qualification as a lawmaker," DPK floor leader Han Byung-do said, referring to Kim. item.title: KOSPI rebounds to close above 7,000 for 1st time in 5 sessions
item.description: KOSPI regained the 7,000 level on Friday, ending above the threshold for the first time in five trading sessions as a late rebound erased earlier losses. The benchmark index added 32.39 points, or 0.46 percent, to finish at 7,003.74. After opening 33.08 points, or 0.47 percent, lower at 6,938.27, it extended its decline to as much as 0.62 percent. The index then swung between gains and losses before moving higher toward the close. Early selling reflected profit-taking ahead of the National Foundation Day holiday and caution over U.S. Treasury yields. item.title: Coupang feared to become 1st target for FTC's investigative task force
item.description: Coupang is facing the prospect of even tougher regulatory scrutiny, as the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) has launched a special investigative task force to investigate complex violations involving dominant platforms, in what appears to be a move targeting the U.S.-listed e-commerce giant. The FTC launched its 40-member Key Investigation Planning Bureau on Thursday, upgrading its existing investigation team to a bureau-level organization dedicated to major cases involving platforms, large business groups and serious violations affecting consumers and small businesses. The new bureau comes as Coupang has emerged as one of the most persistent subjects of FTC scrutiny. With the company increasingly challenging the watchdog’s investigations and actions, their disputes expand across search rankings, supplier transactions, discount costs and its food delivery business. The FTC has not identified its first target, and there is no confirmation that Coupang will be assigned as the first investigation target from the task force. item.title: Seoul pushes for dialogue with NK, but gov't speaks in different tones
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung’s renewed call for dialogue with North Korea following a recent land mine explosion in the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) is highlighting differences in tone within his administration over how to respond to Pyongyang. While the government remains committed to restoring inter-Korean dialogue, Cheong Wa Dae, the unification ministry and the military have differed in how they have addressed North Korea’s responsibility for the incident and how Seoul should respond. Lee referred to the Sept. 21 explosion, which injured three South Korean soldiers, as an “unfortunate accident,” during his Armed Forces Day speech Thursday. Rather than directly blaming North Korea, he called on Pyongyang to “restore trust and resume the dialogue that has been severed.” “Firm security means creating peace in which there is no need to fight,” Lee said, pledging to continue “practical steps” to reduce military tensions. item.title: Could sharing ketchup over french fries be an 'indirect kiss?'
item.description: Click here for more articles by Kormedi.com. Sharing french fries with a friend can sometimes lead to a familiar moment: You take a bite, then plunge the same fry back into the communal ketchup. It may seem harmless, particularly among close friends. Children and teenagers sometimes jokingly call sharing food this way an "indirect kiss." As it turns out, the joke may have a little science behind it. Bacteria from the mouth can indeed make their way into a shared sauce when someone takes a bite and dips the food again, a practice known as "double dipping." But how many double dips would it take to transfer roughly as many bacteria as a 10-second kiss? The answer, based on a playful comparison of findings from separate studies, is around 800,000. Double dipping can transfer oral bacteria Researchers at Clemson University in the United States examined how much bacteria could be transferred when a person bites into food and then dips it back into a shared sauce. Their findings were published in the Journal of Food Safety. The experiment confirmed that bacteria from the mouth can enter the sauce

item.title: Busan moves to secure trademark rights for viral waterfront shark
item.description: When a shark estimated at around two meters in length — believed to be a bronze whaler or dusky shark — drifted unannounced into the harbor off Busan’s North Port, it transformed almost overnight from a surprise guest into a viral mascot for Korea’s second-largest city. Now, municipal officials are stepping in to ensure that the unlikely local celebrity remains a public asset rather than a corporate cash cow. The city government said Friday that it will file trademark applications this month for "Bukangi," the affectionate moniker bestowed upon the shark currently frequenting the North Port Waterfront Park. The decision comes after officials discovered five unauthorized trademark applications filed by a private individual on Sept. 21. The private claims seek exclusive commercial rights over the name in both Korean and English, alongside design graphics covering roughly 40 product categories, including keychains, plush toys and apparel. item.title: 18-month prison term sought for Seoul mayor in appellate political funds trial
item.description: A special counsel team on Friday sought an 18-month prison term for Seoul Mayor Oh Se-hoon in a political funds case over opinion polls conducted in the lead-up to the 2021 mayoral by-election. Special counsel Min Joong-ki's team made the request at the Seoul High Court after a lower court fined Oh 10 million won ($7,400) for violating the Political Funds Act, putting him at risk of losing his mayoral post. Under the law, elected officials are stripped of their seats if they receive a finalized fine of 1 million won or heavier punishment for accepting illegal political funds. Oh was indicted on charges of having a supporter pay 33 million won for opinion poll results he received on 10 occasions from self-proclaimed power broker Myung Tae-kyun ahead of the by-election in April 2021. The lower court partially recognized the charges, ruling that Oh had asked Myung for opinion polls on five occasions and his supporter paid a total of 21 million won. "Defendant Oh Se-hoon is a prominent politician who, more than anyone else, is in a position to follow the Political Funds Act," Min's team said,

item.title: Korean American singer wins appeal in 3rd lawsuit over visa denial
item.description: A court of appeals on Friday upheld a lower court's ruling in favor of Steve Yoo, a Korean American singer, in his third lawsuit seeking to overturn the Korean government's decision to deny him an entry visa after he renounced his Korean citizenship, allegedly to evade mandatory military service. The Seoul High Court ruled that the decision by the Korean Consulate General in Los Angeles to deny Yoo an entry visa must be revoked, upholding a ruling by the Seoul Administrative Court in August last year. The high court did not provide a specific explanation for its ruling. The case is an appeal of Yoo's third lawsuit against the LA consulate general after it denied his visa application. Yoo, 48, also known by his Korean name Yoo Seung-jun, has been barred from entering Korea after he became a U.S. citizen and renounced his Korean citizenship in 2002, with the alleged goal of dodging his military duty. item.title: 2nd rescue attempt to return Busan shark suspended
item.description: A second rescue operation to return “Bukangi,” a shark that has been stranded in an artificial waterway at Busan North Port Waterfront Park for 15 days, to the open sea, has been suspended. A joint rescue team of Busan city officials and other relevant agencies began slowly guiding Bukangi toward the sea at 3 p.m. on Friday, using a 50-meter-long, 6.8-meter-high net and boats positioned on both sides of the waterway. One boat towed the center of the net, while five people were positioned at each end of the waterway to hold the net and keep pace with the shark. Behind the net, another boat equipped with a water pump created foam on the water to guide Bukangi toward the open sea. At around 5:40 p.m., however, the rescue team suspended the operation when the shark was about 50 meters from the sixth pedestrian bridge, which was the last bridge to pass to go toward the open sea. Busan city officials said the operation had become increasingly difficult as the water level rose with high tide approaching, while the net got caught on the bottom about 70 to 80 meters before the sixth pedestria

item.title: Civic group to rally outside actor's home over film 'The Assassin(s)'
item.description: A conservative civic group said Friday it will hold rallies outside the home of actor Yoo Hae-jin to protest alleged historical inaccuracies in his film "The Assassin(s)." The New Freedom Solidarity said it submitted plans to the police to stage rallies outside Yoo's home in northern Seoul at 4:30 p.m. every day starting Saturday until the end of the month. The movie, which features Yoo in a leading role, deals with the 1974 assassination of former first lady Yuk Young-soo, the wife of late former President Park Chung-hee. It has drawn intense backlash from conservative groups and politicians, who argue the film maliciously implies Park was behind the incident. "We are asking the actor to also appear in right-wing movies so that there is a political balance," Kim Sang-jin, the leader of the civic group, told Yonhap News Agency. "There are many things we could raise suspicions about too, and we want him to appear in (films about them) too." The film's production team has said the work was not intended to draw a new historical conclusion or deny or distort established facts.

item.title: From screen to street food, Korea brings its dynamic storytellers to London
item.description: London is set to spend October immersed in contemporary Korean culture, with dramas, literature and food brought together for a monthlong program featuring screenings, author talks and Korean street-food experiences. The Korean Cultural Centre UK said Friday that Curated Korea 2026 will introduce works, creators and ideas shaping Korean culture through programs spanning television, books and food. The program opened Thursday with a screening and discussion of Tving original drama “The Ordinary Jackpot” at the Korean Cultural Centre, which will be followed by a screening of “Study Group” at Foyles Charing Cross on Oct. 8. Renowned K-drama director Jang Tae-yoo — best known for hits like "My Love from the Star" — will attend a screening and Q&A session for his upcoming series “Bon Appétit, Your Majesty” at the Royal Society of Arts on Oct. 9. item.title: CJ ENM wins 7 national titles at Asian Academy Creative Awards
item.description: CJ ENM won national winner titles in seven categories at this year's Asian Academy Creative Awards and will compete for the top regional prizes in December, the Korean entertainment company said Friday. "The Legend of Kitchen Soldier," a military kitchen comedy on CJ ENM's streaming platform Tving, took two titles — best comedy and best original production by a streamer. "Bon Appétit, Your Majesty," a romance streaming on Netflix about a modern chef who travels back in time to cook for a Joseon-era king, won best drama series. "Dear X," a Tving thriller directed by Lee Eung-bok, won best direction for a scripted program, while Lee Won-woong's boxing survival show "I Am Boxer," which streams on Disney+, won the nonscripted direction category. "Undercover Chef" won best general entertainment, game or quiz program, and the dating reality show "EXchange 4" won best nonscripted entertainment. item.title: HD Hyundai Heavy Industries wins contract for 500-MW offshore substation in Taean
item.description: HD Hyundai Heavy Industries has signed a contract to build an offshore substation for a wind farm in waters off Taean, South Chungcheong Province, as it expands its presence in the offshore wind market. The company announced on Friday that it recently signed a contract with Taean Wind Power to carry out the engineering, procurement, fabrication, installation and commissioning of an offshore substation for the wind farm. Taean Wind Power is a joint venture between Singapore-based renewable energy company Vena Energy, Danish investment and development firm Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) and state-run Korea Western Power. An offshore substation is a key facility that transmits electricity generated by turbines at an offshore wind farm to shore. The offshore substation to be built in Taean will step up the voltage of electricity generated by a 500-megawatt wind farm before transmitting the power to shore. HD Hyundai Heavy Industries secured the project through a series of agreements, signing a front-end engineering design contract in March, followed by a preferred supplier agreement

item.title: S. Korea, Ukraine's FMs discuss 'proper message' on NK POW transfer dispute: senior official
item.description: The South Korean and Ukrainian foreign ministers have been discussing how Kyiv should respond to South Korea's demand for an apology over the disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul, a senior government official here said Friday. The South Korean government demanded an official explanation and apology over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent disclosure of the transfer and a statement from his office denying that there had been an agreement to keep the matter confidential. item.title: Border tensions cost South Korean frontier counties $22 mil. in tourism, damage
item.description: South Korea's border regions saw tourism spending fall by more than 30 billion won ($22 million) and reported hundreds of millions of won in direct damage during 2024 and 2025, when North Korea's trash-filled balloon launches and tit-for-tat loudspeaker broadcasts under the former Yoon Suk Yeol administration escalated inter-Korean tensions. According to the data submitted by Gyeonggi and Gangwon provinces to the office of Woo Won-shik of the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) on Friday, Gyeonggi Province reported a total of 24 incidents of damage worth 414.42 million won across 10 cities and counties as a result of North Korea’s waste balloon launches between May 28, 2024, and November 28, 2025. Border regions also experienced a sharp decline in tourism spending during the same period. item.title: 99.3% of soybeans imported from US test positive for genetic modification
item.description: Genetically modified organism (GMO) components were detected in 99.3 percent of U.S. soybean import cases tested over the past decade, trade data showed Friday, raising calls for Korea to diversify its soybean import sources. According to Korea Agro-Fisheries & Food Trade Corp. data submitted to Rep. Song Ok-joo of the Democratic Party of Korea, Korea imported 1.6 million tons of U.S. soybeans between 2017 and September 2026, accounting for 91.5 percent of its total soybean imports during the period. GMO components were detected in 399 of 402 U.S. soybean import cases, or 99.3 percent. Canadian soybeans were imported in 45 shipments totaling 29,469 tons, with GMO components detected in 57.8 percent of the cases. In contrast, no GMO components were detected in soybeans imported from China or Russia. Chinese soybeans totaled 112,124 tons in 18 shipments, accounting for 6.4 percent of total imports, while Russian soybeans totaled 7,870 tons across five shipments. The data came amid recent controversies over GMO detection in soybean-based foods such as tofu, soy milk and fermented soybean pa

item.title: Upbit adds AI tools that explain crypto price moves
item.description: Dunamu, the operator of Korea’s largest cryptocurrency exchange Upbit, said Friday that it expanded its artificial intelligence (AI)-powered market analytics platform with real-time tools that summarize broad market trends and pinpoint the reasons behind price movements for individual digital assets. Upbit Data Lab, launched in April 2025, is the exchange's analytics platform offering crypto indexes, sector data and blockchain analysis. The new "AI Market Report" is a video of 90 seconds or less that draws on the Upbit composite index, major asset prices, top gainers and losers, and market sentiment indicators, with AI selecting key issues based on price moves and market impact. It is released at 10 a.m. on weekdays on Upbit Data Lab and Upbit's official YouTube channel. A second new service, "Uptrace," tracks price data and related news for individual assets to identify the main factors behind price changes. item.title: Seoul looks to foreign entrepreneurs to fuel its next economic engine
item.description: Armed with an artificial intelligence (AI) platform designed to predict fall risks for the elderly, a Ukrainian entrepreneur walked away from a Seoul pitch competition this week with something far more valuable than cash: a golden ticket toward permanent residency in Korea. The winning startup, NeuroDetectYO, was named top entry at Seoul’s second annual "Jump Up, Start Up" foreign entrepreneurship competition. Founder Oleksandr Yuhai received a 2 million won ($1,500) cash reward, but the most crucial prize was 30 points toward Korea’s notoriously difficult D-8-4 technology startup visa — a vital bridge allowing foreign founders to convert ambitious ideas into permanent Korean businesses. As domestic birth rates plummet and economic growth slows, Seoul is aggressively pivoting outward, attempting to transform itself into Asia's premier hub for global tech talent. City officials are actively rolling out the red carpet for foreign founders, believing that international perspectives can ignite the capital’s next wave of growth. item.title: College students' living expense loans increase amid soaring housing, food costs
item.description: "I make about 600,000 won ($440) a month from my part-time job at a cafe. Even with a little help from my parents, I can't cover my rent and living expenses," said Kim, a college student living in Seongbuk District, Seoul. "I've been asking my friends about income requirements and other eligibility criteria because I'm considering taking out a loan from the Korea Student Aid Foundation (KOSAF) next semester," she said. Kim's concerns reflect a broader trend, with living-expense loans taken out by college students surging by nearly one-third over the past two years, while overdue balances also rose sharply, data showed Thursday. The amount of living-expense loans extended to university students by KOSAF rose 32.8 percent to 850.6 billion won ($626.5 million) in 2025 from 640.67 billion won in 2023, according to data submitted by KOSAF to Rep. Kang Kyung-sook of the Rebuilding Korea Party. The number of loans also increased from 432,171 to 457,129 over the same period. item.title: [K-ART FOCUS] For Dew Kim, K-pop, faith and queer bodies meet onstage
item.description: JEONNAM-GWANGJU SPECIAL METROPOLITAN CITY — A pink microphone, a K-pop light stick and a glowing circular light each crown three white, soft-edged bodies that may be either collapsing into or growing out of the floor, entangled in chains and pierced by spindly metal structures with smartphone screens. The figure in Dew Kim’s “Legion, Nowhere Whole” (2026) evokes images of wounded idols, saints and soldiers. One form resembles a horse, another suggests a person or an animal caught in a moment of metamorphosis. Together, they form Kim’s response to a world in which people are continually asked to put themselves on display through social media, performance and the pursuit of recognition. “The title was inspired by Roman legions and soldiers,” Kim said in an interview with The Korea Times. “They were expected to fight until their bodies were no longer intact. I thought that was similar to how we are constantly required to show ourselves, to be recognized and validated, until there is almost no part of the body left whole.” The work is part of “The Look is A Li(k)e” at

item.title: Human prism: Lee Byung-hun
item.description: Between “G.I. Joe” and “ Squid Game,” hero and villain, acclaim and controversy, actor Lee Byung-hun has made the space between worlds a stage for his brilliance. A defining figure of Korean cinema, he absorbs the light and shadow of his time, refracting contradictory elements of desires and anxiety through his life and performance. A recent Forbes headline offered an unexpected point of connection: “Oracle Has Cut 21,000 Jobs This Year Due to AI, More Layoffs Expected.” The news of workers confronting an uncertain future echoed themes that emerged in a long conversation with Lee last year — a broader exploration of the human condition in an age when familiar boundaries are increasingly difficult to hold. On a crisp October day, with late autumn settling quietly over Seoul, Lee sat down for an extended conversation at a quiet cafe in Samcheong-dong. The meeting followed a series of encounters at the Venice International Film Festival, in Los Angeles and later in Busan, before the conversation finally continued in Seoul. item.title: Traditional fireworks tours to draw 1,800 Japanese visitors to Andong, Haman
item.description: About 1,800 Japanese travelers are heading to Andong and Haman this month on specialized tours built around centuries-old flame festivals, marking a major government effort to drive foreign tourism into historic regions located 190 to 280 kilometers south of Seoul, the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Tourism Organization (KTO) said Friday. In Andong, North Gyeongsang Province, about 300 visitors will watch "Hahoe Seonyu Julbul Nori" on five dates through the end of October. In the tradition, which dates to the Joseon Dynasty (1392-1910), pouches of charcoal powder hung on ropes over the Nakdong River burn slowly, showering sparks onto the water at Hahoe Folk Village, a UNESCO World Heritage site. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi watched the display in May during a summit with President Lee Jae Myung in Andong. The package, developed by the KTO's Japan offices and the Japan Association of Travel Agents, includes a dedicated viewing zone and traditional souvenirs. item.title: Seokguram exhibition opens in Paris to mark 140 years of Korea-France ties
item.description: An exhibition on Seokguram Grotto, an eighth-century Buddhist cave temple among Korea's first UNESCO World Heritage sites, opened in Paris on Thursday (local time), alongside a weeklong Korean heritage festival, the Korea Heritage Service (KHS) said Friday. The exhibition, "The Millennium Mystery of Buddhist Art: Seokguram," runs through March 13, 2027, at the Korean Cultural Center in France. The KHS organized it with the center and the Gyeongju city government to mark the 140th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Korea and France. Seokguram is an artificial granite grotto on Mount Toham in Gyeongju, the capital of the Silla Kingdom (57 B.C.-A.D. 935). It was added to the UNESCO list in 1995. The show features a 3D immersive video recreating the grotto's interior and a reconstruction of green-glazed tiles depicting Buddhist guardian deities that once decorated a wooden pagoda base at the Sacheonwang Temple Site in Gyeongju. Korean Ambassador to France Kwon Hyuk-woon gave opening remarks, followed by congratulatory speeches from Rep. Kim Seok-ki, Gyeongju Mayor Joo Nak-young and

item.title: K-brands gain new shield against overseas counterfeits
item.description: As global demand for K-beauty, K-food and K-fashion soars, Korea is launching a joint government crackdown to protect small businesses from overseas knockoffs and trademark theft. The Ministry of SMEs and Startups and the Korean Intellectual Property Office said Friday they will launch a joint council to share cases of trademark and design infringement and coordinate support for small businesses expanding overseas. The council held its inaugural meeting Friday afternoon at Government Complex Daejeon, bringing together the ministry, Korea SMEs and Startups Agency, Korean Intellectual Property Office and Korea Intellectual Property Protection Agency. The agencies said they will use overseas centers operated by the Korea SMEs and Startups Agency and overseas intellectual property centers operated by the Korean Intellectual Property Protection Agency to share information and respond to cases involving unauthorized trademark registrations, counterfeits and other infringements. item.title: Lee warns of 'additional measures' if Ukraine refuses to apologize for NK POW transfer disclosure
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung warned Friday that South Korea will take "additional measures" should Ukraine continue to refuse to officially apologize for denying its agreement to keep the transfer of North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) secret. The South Korean president issued the warning on his X account amid a diplomatic wrangle with Ukraine over Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's surprise disclosure last week of the transfer of two North Korean POWs to South Korea. Seoul has since accused Ukraine of breaching a bilateral agreement to keep the transfer secret, but Ukraine has denied the existence of the confidentiality agreement. "If (Ukraine) continues to deny the fact and refuse to offer an official apology, (Seoul) will take additional measures," Lee said. Lee affirmed that Ukraine unilaterally disclosed the transfer despite having previously demanded confidentiality from South Korea, and then made the head of state of the counterpart country a "liar" by saying the nondisclosure agreement did not exist. item.title: Unification minister proposes talks with N. Korea over border line amid DMZ tensions
item.description: Unification Minister Chung Dong-young on Friday proposed to North Korea talks to address issues along the border, amid heightened inter-Korean tensions over last week's mine blast inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ). Chung made the remark after the South's military blamed North Korea for the Sept. 21 land mine explosion on the South's side of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) separating the two Koreas. The incident left three South Korean soldiers injured, two of them critically. Earlier this week, the South Korean military demanded an apology and responsible measures from the North over the blast. Pyongyang has categorically denied its involvement, accusing Seoul of fabricating its investigation result to pin the blame on the regime. "The root cause of this incident ultimately lies in the issue of the ceasefire line, the MDL line," Chung told reporters upon arriving for work. He cut short his trip to Europe and returned Thursday to handle the fallout from the land mine blast. "I, as unification minister, propose to the North: We should meet now and communicate. item.title: Jim Carrey reportedly weds girlfriend believed to be of Korean descent
item.description: Hollywood star Jim Carrey has reportedly tied the knot for a third time, marrying his partner Min Ah, who is 32 years his junior, in a private ceremony in Los Angeles. Multiple U.S. entertainment outlets, including TMZ and People, reported Wednesday that Carrey recently held a small, private wedding ceremony in Los Angeles. Min Ah has been described as being of Korean descent, although her Korean heritage has not been officially confirmed. The couple reportedly began dating in 2022 but kept their relationship largely out of the public eye. They made their first official public appearance together in February at the César Awards in Paris, France. Carrey received an honorary award at the ceremony and publicly acknowledged Min Ah during his acceptance speech, describing her as his "sublime companion" and saying that he loved her. The marriage marks another chapter in the personal life of the 64-year-old actor, one of Hollywood's most recognizable comedy stars. item.description: Global K-pop phenomenon BTS has been designated "honorary guests" of Bogota, an official honor recognizing the group's contribution to culture and youth influence, ahead of the start of its Latin American tour, the group's label said Friday. BigHit Music said the title was conferred by the mayor of Bogota, the capital of Colombia, on the septet for helping raise the international profile of Korean music and culture since its 2013 debut and influencing younger generations. The honor is given to prominent visitors who have contributed to citizens' welfare or urban development in various fields, such as politics, public service, the arts, sports, science and education. item.title: Gov't to consider further reducing Treasury bond issuance if necessary: finance minister
item.description: The finance minister on Friday said Korea will consider further reducing Treasury bond issuance if necessary, pledging to continue closely monitoring the market. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il's remark came after Korea decided to reduce Treasury bond issuance by 5 trillion won ($3.64 billion) in October, with the government also pledging to implement stabilization measures, including emergency bond buybacks, if needed. Lee discussed the issue during a meeting with Bank of Korea Gov. Shin Hyun-song, Financial Services Commission Chairman Lee Eog-weon, Financial Supervisory Service Gov. Lee Chan-jin and Land Minister Hong Jee-sun. It marked the first meeting of its kind since Lee took office last month. item.title: Seoul shares narrow losses late Fri. morning on tech gains
item.description: Seoul shares narrowed their losses late Friday morning as investors engaged in profit-taking while scooping up major technology stocks ahead of the holiday. After opening 0.47 percent lower, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) gained 16.72 points, or 0.24 percent, to 6,977.07 as of 11:20 a.m. The market will be closed Monday for a national holiday. Overnight, U.S. stocks finished modestly higher as benchmark Treasury yields eased from fresh multi-decade highs, although gains were capped by rising crude oil prices. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 0.04 percent, while the benchmark S&P 500 gained 0.19 percent. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite added 0.04 percent. In Seoul, market heavyweights were trading mixed. Top market cap Samsung Electronics inched up 0.09 percent, and chip giant SK hynix gained 0.44 percent. SK Square, the parent company of SK hynix, declined 0.43 percent, while Samsung Electro-Mechanics, an electronics component affiliate of Samsung Electronics, inched down 0.13 percent. item.title: N. Korea's FM calls for stronger ties with China in letter to Wang Yi
item.description: North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui has called for efforts to further strengthen bilateral ties and traditional friendship with China in a congratulatory message to her Chinese counterpart, Wang Yi, Pyongyang's state media reported Friday. Choe sent the message to Wang on Thursday marking the 77th anniversary of China's founding, praising the country's achievements over the past seven decades, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). Choe said North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Chinese President Xi Jinping reaffirmed their "steadfast will" to build a better future for their peoples together during their summit talks in Pyongyang in June. The minister also expressed a commitment to working together to fully implement important agreements reached by the leaders and further develop bilateral friendly relations to a "higher stage." Earlier, Kim sent a congratulatory message to Xi on the anniversary and expressed his willingness to further develop relations and safeguard their common interests, the KCNA reported Thursday.

item.title: Hyundai, Kia post record US sales in September
item.description: Hyundai Motor Co. and Kia Corp. posted record U.S. sales for September, driven by strong demand for sport utility vehicles (SUVs) and hybrid models, the Hyundai Motor Group affiliates said Friday. Hyundai Motor America sold 77,439 vehicles last month, up 9 percent from a year earlier, marking its highest-ever September sales. Sales of the Palisade SUV surged 52 percent on-year, while the Sonata, Tucson and Santa Fe also posted double-digit growth. Hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) accounted for 28 percent of Hyundai's total U.S. sales during the month. Kia America also reported its best-ever September sales, with deliveries jumping 18 percent on-year to 77,009 units. The Seltos, Niro, K4, Telluride, Sorento, Carnival, K5 and Sportage were among the models that contributed to the strong monthly performance.

item.title: Consumer prices up 2.9% in September
item.description: Korea's consumer prices rose 2.9 percent in September from a year earlier, data showed Friday, with energy costs remaining elevated while prices of agricultural goods declined. According to data from the Ministry of Data and Statistics, consumer price growth returned to 2 percent levels in September. The consumer price increase came to 2.8 percent in July and 3.1 percent in August. The latest report was released at a time when prices of petroleum products remained elevated amid the prolonged geopolitical tension in the Middle East, rising 14.8 percent on-year in September. In detail, diesel prices rose sharply by 20 percent, and gasoline prices shot up 11.8 percent. Korea relies heavily on imports to meet its energy needs. The government, meanwhile, said the fuel price cap currently in place is estimated to have limited the overall increase in consumer prices by 0.6 percentage point. The report showed that prices of overall industrial products rose 4.2 percent from a year earlier in September. item.title: US sanctions target Iran's auto, rail sectors as blockade chokes ship lanes
item.description: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration imposed sanctions on Iran's rail and auto sectors and their foreign suppliers, the Treasury Department said on Thursday, widening its wartime economic campaign to isolate Tehran. The sanctions are part of the department's "Operation Economic Outcast," announced August 24, which aims to cut Tehran's funding for the war, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps or IRGC. The move extends U.S. economic pressure on Iran from sea to land, targeting sectors Tehran has leaned on since a naval blockade cut off its oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. But the expanding sanctions risk inflicting severe costs on ordinary Iranians, one analyst said. The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports has forced Tehran to rely more on autos and rail for transporting petroleum, fertilizer, chemicals and other goods. Thursday's sanctions target those alternatives, according to the Treasury Department. item.title: Korea abolishes Prosecutors' Office after 78 years, putting new criminal justice system to test
item.description: Korea on Friday abolished the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office after 78 years and launched two new state agencies dividing its investigative and prosecutorial powers, ushering in one of the most sweeping changes to the country’s criminal justice system in decades. Under the new framework taking effect Friday, investigations will be divided among the newly established Serious Crimes Investigation Agency (SCIA), the police and the Corruption Investigation Office for High-ranking Officials (CIO). The new Prosecution Service will review cases, decide whether to indict suspects, request warrants from courts based on applications from investigative agencies and conduct prosecutions in court. But the launch of the new system leaves several unanswered questions: How agencies will handle cases when their jurisdictions overlap, whether prosecutors can exercise sufficient oversight without investigative authority of their own and whether the new agencies are adequately staffed and equipped to take over complex major-crime investigations. item.title: [K-LIT REVIEW] 'Bonobo' asks who is the noble beast?
item.description: "Bonobo," Jeong Yoo-jeong's latest book to be translated to English, does not pull punches. Whether physical or emotional, battles are fought with animal intensity and have lasting impact. The most devastating punch of all, however, is how often we do nothing for someone in need. “I pretended I hadn’t heard,” and “Go ask someone else,” aren’t just quotes from the novel — they are the chorus of an unsympathetic world. Can the three main characters teach us how to help? The book presents a well-worn sci-fi plot point: a transfer of consciousness from one body to another. A car crash throws the psyche of primatologist Jini into the mind of a bonobo. As she struggles to find her way back to her own body, Jini also experiences the primate's memories of captivity and trafficking, forcing her to reconsider the relationship between humans and animals. As the book teaches us about bonobos through Jini, we also learn about her own self-doubt and skepticism regarding human nature. Who is a "noble beast, and who is a terrible animal? A moment of birth is a shared joy for a bonobo fami

item.title: Trump vows to hit Iran 'very hard' if linked to FlyDubai attack
item.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump warned on Thursday that Iran will be "hit very hard" if it is found to be linked to a pilot's attack on a flydubai flight to Israel. The dramatic events a day earlier saw passengers help stop the plane from crashing, making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia before the flight's mostly Israeli passengers were flown home to a hero's welcome. Trump's warning came as the United Arab Emirates opened an investigation into whether the incident was linked to terrorism and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the suspect had undergone "Islamist radical indoctrination." "I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes but we're working on it right now," Trump told reporters Thursday when asked at the White House whether Iran was involved in what happened on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. On whether the United States would retaliate against Iran if it was found responsible, Trump replied: "Oh, they'll be hit very hard, don't worry." item.title: Why copilot attacked captain of Israel-bound flight remains unknown
item.description: JERUSALEM — Investigators worked Thursday to determine why an Omani pilot stabbed the captain of a flight to Israel, causing the plane to plummet dangerously before others on board landed it in Saudi Arabia. Passengers on the FlyDubai plane — which was carrying 174 people, mostly Israelis, from the United Arab Emirates to Tel Aviv — have described how the bloodied Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door to let them in before they grappled with the copilot and stabilized a descent so sharp that the plane’s rudder was torn away. “We felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didn’t know who to turn to. But it was all instinct to survive,” Asaf Rajuan, who was among those who intervened, said in a statement shared by Israel’s presidency. A regional official briefed on the investigation said the suspect, an Omani citizen, was under arrest and confirmed that Saudi authorities were working with countries, including Israel, to try to determine a motive. item.title: Cornell and Burning Sun: What's behind the comparisons?
item.description: SEATTLE — The sexual assault allegations involving seven current and former Cornell University students are drawing comparisons to Korea’s Burning Sun scandal, with parallels focusing on private group chats, male group dynamics and questions of institutional accountability. The Cornell case centers on allegations that a female student was drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024. A civil lawsuit filed last month names seven current and former students, including Winston Lee, whose ties to Korea have drawn particular attention in Korean and Korean American online communities. Burning Sun erupted in 2019 as one of Korea’s most notorious scandals in recent years, growing from allegations surrounding a Seoul nightclub into a sprawling case involving prostitution, sexual violence, illegally filmed and disseminated sexual videos, gambling and allegations of police corruption. item.title: US Supreme Court to review indefinite immigrant detention
item.description: WASHINGTON — The U.S. Supreme Court said Thursday it will decide whether President Donald Trump's administration can deny immigrants facing deportation the chance to seek release on bond, in the latest major challenge to his hardline immigration agenda. The policy, introduced after Trump returned to office last year, allows authorities to keep some immigrants detained throughout removal proceedings — potentially for years — even if they have lived in the United States for decades. Previous administrations, including Trump's first, generally allowed such detainees to ask an immigration judge for release while their cases were decided, provided they were not considered dangerous or likely to flee. The administration argues that a 1996 immigration law requires mandatory detention for people who entered the country illegally, regardless of how long ago they arrived. Immigrant advocates say that provision was intended chiefly for people stopped at or near the border and that long-term residents arrested inside the country should remain eligible for bond hearings. item.title: Family of woman killed by US immigration agent sues Trump administration
item.description: WASHINGTON — The family of Renee Good, an unarmed U.S. citizen shot dead by an immigration agent during a sweeping federal crackdown, sued President Donald Trump's administration on Thursday, alleging wrongful death and civil rights violations. Good, 37, was killed in Minneapolis on January 7 when an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent fired three shots into her car during Operation Metro Surge, the administration's mass deployment in Minnesota. Her family filed two lawsuits in federal court. One names the United States and seeks damages under the Federal Tort Claims Act, alleging wrongful death, negligence and other misconduct. The second names the killer, Jonathan Ross, along with senior Trump administration officials including then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller. Both Trump officials baselessly accused Good of terrorism, with Noem falsely claiming in a press conference that the victim had "attempted to run a law enforcement officer over." item.title: 'It's not that we like Seoul': Young Koreans explain why they leave their hometowns
item.description: "Why do you insist on living in Seoul? You could just live in your own region." Young people from outside the capital hear that question often, and they say it misses the point. About 30,000 of them move to Seoul each year in net terms for university or work, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics. The regional antagonism that split their parents' generation between the Jeolla provinces in Korea's southwest and the Gyeongsang provinces in the southeast has faded. In its place, the concentration of opportunity in Seoul alone has deepened their marginalization. Eight participants in a roundtable discussion described what that gap looks like from the other end of the country. item.title: 1st-gen K-pop is coming back as Fin.K.L, Fly to the Sky, Son Ho-young return
item.description: As K-pop's newest generation competes for attention, some of the industry's original stars are stepping back into the spotlight. Fin.K.L, Fly to the Sky and g.o.d's Son Ho-young are all preparing new music activities, bringing a wave of first-generation K-pop nostalgia to an industry now dominated by much younger acts. The returns are particularly notable because they are not limited to performances of old hits: The veteran artists are preparing new releases and longer-term activities after years away from their respective music careers. Fin.K.L, one of the defining girl groups of K-pop's first generation, is making a full-group return after about 21 years. Gemstone E&M, which is overseeing the group's comeback, announced Sept. 21 that all four members — Lee Hyo-ri, Ock Joo-hyun, Sung Yu-ri and Lee Jin — would resume activities together. It marks Fin.K.L's first full-fledged group activities since the 2005 digital single "Forever Fin.K.L." item.title: "The School That Became a Grave": Jeremy Scahill on U.S Bombing of Minab, Killing 120+ Iranian Kids
item.description:
Drop Site News released a major investigation this week into the U.S. bombing of the Shajareh Tayyebeh children’s school in the Iranian city of Minab on February 28, the first day of the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran. Drop Site spoke to survivors, first responders, parents and witnesses in one of the most in-depth reports on the massacre to date. The bombing killed at least 156 people — 120 of the victims were children, 26 were teachers, and the rest were parents. A United Nations fact-finding mission recently concluded that the U.S. strike was a war crime, but the Trump administration has not yet even acknowledged U.S. responsibility.

“This was not a single bombing or collateral damage,” says Drop Site News’s Jeremy Scahill, lead author of the investigation. “There were at least two direct hits on a school packed with children … and a couple of hours after those initial hits, as first responders came, as parents came, the U.S. launches more strikes.”

Scahill points out that until 2013, the area where the school is was a facility operated by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps. But in satellite photos from just weeks before the strike, “You could see the murals on the wall. You could see the soccer field. Some of the satellite photos show shadows of tiny people playing outside.”

item.title: "Cruel & Torturous": Christa Pike in Critical Condition After Botched Tennessee Execution
item.source:markdown:
Tennessee’s Governor Bill Lee has halted executions for the remainder of the year after a death row prisoner survived two lethal injections on Wednesday. According to her lawyers, Christa Pike was still breathing after she was strapped to a gurney and injected with two syringes of pentobarbital in a botched execution that spanned more than two hours. Prior to the scheduled execution, Pike and her lawyers argued a single-dose lethal injection could be tantamount to torture due to Pike’s small veins. Pike was sentenced to death for a 1995 murder she committed when she was 18. Now in the hospital in critical condition, she is the first person to ever survive lethal injection in the United States.
“I have seen five executions in Tennessee,” says Steven Hale, a criminal justice reporter for the _Nashville Banner_, who witnessed Christa Pike’s botched execution. “And I’ve never seen anything like what we saw Wednesday night.”
Christa Pike “has just experienced the most agonizing attempt at lethal injection in the country’s history,” says Sandra Babcock, director of the Cornell Center on the Death Penalty Worldwide. Babcock says Pike should have never been sentenced to death, because she was an “immature 18-year-old” with a history of severe childhood and sexual trauma who “was not receiving medication for post-traumatic stress disorder and bipolar disorder at the time of \[the murder\], which she committed with her abusive boyfriend at the time.”

item.title: Why are B.C. firefighters still using wildfire data from the 1990s?
item.description: Prolonged drought in B.C.'s Southern Interior has led to explosive wildfires that current modelling software struggles to predict. item.source:markdown:
![Neal McLoughlin, the Supt. of Predictive Services at the BC Wildfire Service says his team has learned to be skeptical of their fire modelling software's predictions during hot and dry days because the models underperform.](https://i.cbc.ca/ais/7087d69e-7668-4ab7-9ff5-0274c418eb98,1790789182101/full/max/0/default.jpg?im=Crop%2Crect%3D%280%2C208%2C4000%2C2250%29%3B)

item.title: Iran's Revolutionary Guards kill six 'terrorists' in restive region, IRNA news agency reports
item.description: Iran's Revolutionary Guards killed six members of a "terrorist" group on Thursday, the IRNA state news agency reported, in a region often hit by clashes between the security forces and armed groups, including Sunni militants and separatists. The killings occurred in Zahedan, capital of the impoverished Sistan-Baluchistan province in southeastern Iran, which borders Pakistan and Afghanistan and is a major drug trafficking route. The IRNA report said security forces had discovered and confiscated explosive packages. It did not identify the six people killed and gave no further information on the incident. Tehran accuses some armed groups of ties to foreign powers and involvement in cross-border smuggling. Human rights group Haalvsh, which monitors Sistan-Baluchistan, said fighting between military and security forces and armed individuals had started on Thursday morning. Separately, the sound of an explosion was heard on Wednesday in Zahedan without causing any damage, Fars news agency reported, citing the city's administrative office. The reports came as Tehran weighs a U.S. response to its

item.title: Netanyahu says Flydubai co-pilot underwent Islamist radical indoctrination
item.description: WASHINGTON — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Thursday that the co-pilot who tried to crash a passenger jet on its way to Israel had undergone Islamist radicalization. "We know that he underwent Islamist radical indoctrination," Netanyahu said in an interview with Fox News. No motive has been determined for Wednesday's harrowing near-disaster on Wednesday's Flydubai flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv, when passengers were able to subdue the attacker and a reserve crew aboard landed the plane in Saudi Arabia. Netanyahu told "Fox & Friends" he would be able to say within a matter of days whether the flydubai co-pilot had connections to Iran. "I think it's too early to say whether he had any connections with Iran or with any anyone else," he said. Netanyahu said it was clear that the co-pilot was suicidal. "If you couple that with the what I just told you about the Islamist tendencies, that radicalization that are found in his background, I think that's — that'll give us the a pretty good clue," he said. "But again, I don't make final conclusions yet. But that's the ind

item.title: Breturn? Wary EU waits for actions, not words from UK
item.description: BRUSSELS — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham may have shifted the dial by floating a return for his country to the European Union. But after a rollercoaster decade since the Brexit vote, the U.K. rejoining is only a distant prospect and Brussels is waiting first to see what London wants next. "It's positive. It improves the tone," one EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told AFP. "But we're not going to change our approach because there's nice music in the background." Burnham — who took power in July — this week broke a taboo for a British premier by opening the door to the U.K.'s possible return to the fold. Smashing through red lines set by his cautious predecessor Keir Starmer, the former mayor of Manchester said potential options might include staying as is, joining the EU's customs union or single market, or eventually going "all the way." The positive vibes from the new UK leader drew a warm response from several of his European counterparts. "Welcome back," quipped French President Emmanuel Macron in English. "If the British want to come back and if the prime min

item.title: Drone crash mars weapon demonstration on Armed Forces Day
item.description: A target drone crashed during a live demonstration of Korea’s domestically developed laser air-defense weapon during the nation’s Armed Forces Day ceremony on Wednesday. The incident occurred during a military ceremony held on the runway at Gyeryongdae, the military headquarters complex in Gyeryong, South Chungcheong Province. President Lee Jae Myung, Defense Minister Kang Shin-cheol and National Assembly Speaker Cho Jeong-sik were among the dignitaries attending the event. Four fiber-optic drones were deployed as targets in the demonstration, which was intended to show the Cheongwang laser weapon’s ability to intercept airborne threats. In the first sequence, one of two target drones lost balance and crashed during takeoff. The incident was captured in a close-up camera shot and broadcast live. According to the military, the drone, which is controlled using a thin fiber-optic cable rather than radio signals, crashed after strong gusts damaged the cable. item.title: Tennessee governor halts executions after Christa Gail Pike survives lethal injection attempt
item.description: NASHVILLE, Tenn. — Tennessee officials were unable to put Christa Gail Pike to death Wednesday for a 1995 murder after administering two doses of a lethal drug. A death penalty expert said it was an unprecedented failure, and Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee halted the one remaining execution for the rest of the year. Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and taken by ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital, but they said they hadn’t been told about her condition. She had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start and hours later the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay. Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday. Gov. item.title: BTS becomes 1st pop group to surpass $500 mil. in tour ticket sales
item.description: Global K-pop sensation BTS has become the first pop group in the world to surpass $500 million in cumulative ticket sales with its ongoing "Arirang" world tour, Billboard said. The South Korean septet's tour was the seventh by any group to reach the milestone, the U.S. music industry publication said, citing its latest Boxscore figures released Wednesday (U.S. time). "It puts them in unprecedented territory as a pop group, as the other six ensembles are all rock bands," Billboard added. Much of this milestone was driven by recent shows. In August alone — about four months after the tour began in South Korea in April — BTS staged 12 concerts, drawing about 800,000 fans and generating $171.7 million in ticket sales, according to the figures. This performance put the group at the top of Billboard's monthly Top Tours chart for the fifth time, placing it behind Bad Bunny with 10 No. 1 finishes, and Beyonce, Coldplay and Elton John with seven each. The group's August revenue was also the second-highest monthly total in Billboard Boxscore history, behind Beyonce's figure from August 2023. Wit

item.title: Nat'l Assembly passes bill introducing profit-based penalties over workplace deaths
item.description: The National Assembly on Thursday passed a revised bill imposing financial penalties on companies over fatal industrial accidents to better protect workers and strengthen workplace safety. The revision to the Occupational Safety and Health Act passed in a 161-52 vote with six abstentions during a parliamentary plenary session, despite objections from the main opposition People Power Party (PPP). The revision calls for imposing a fine of up to five percent of the company's operating profit for violating safety regulations when three or more workers die in industrial accidents within a year. The PPP has argued that the five percent threshold would be excessive, citing the financial burden it could place on companies, while the ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) has criticized the PPP for blocking the bill to protect corporate interests rather than workers. "The conditions are already difficult for companies to grow," PPP chief spokesperson Rep. Choi Soo-jin told reporters before the plenary session. "We clearly oppose the bill because we believe it places a burden on companies." During

item.title: Samsung Bioepis, Teva enter commercialization agreement on 6 biosimilar candidates
item.description: Samsung Bioepis and Teva Pharmaceutical Industries have entered into an agreement on commercializing the former’s up to six potential biosimilar candidates, including two confirmed investigational candidates, the companies said Thursday. According to Samsung Bioepis, the two sides have signed a global licensing, development and commercialization agreement for the potential candidates. Of them, two confirmed investigational biosimilar candidates are SB41, referencing AstraZeneca’s Fasenra, a treatment primarily used for severe eosinophilic asthma, and SB44, referencing Novartis’ Ilaris, which treats a range of inflammatory conditions including rare autoinflammatory diseases. Under the terms of the agreement, Samsung Bioepis will be responsible for the development, regulatory registration and manufacturing of the biosimilars, while Teva will be responsible for commercialization in global markets, including the U.S., Europe and Canada. item.title: Homer Hulbert to be honored with bust in his Vermont birthplace
item.description: Homer Hulbert (1863-1949), an American educator and missionary who devoted his life to Korea independence, will be honored with a bust in his home state of Vermont, the Hulbert Memorial Society (HMS) said Wednesday. According to HMS, the unveiling ceremony will take place Saturday in New Haven, Vermont. The bust will be flanked by two stone monuments bearing inscriptions in Korean and English. "We hope they will serve as a lasting reminder of what Hulbert did for Korea and of friendship between Korea and the U.S.," HMS Chairman Kim Dong-jin said in a press release. Korean sculptor Kwon Chi-gyu made the 180-centimeter-tall bronze bust in Korea, which was then shipped to Vermont. The monuments were made with stones native to the area. Vermont Governor Philip Scott, state Sen. Ruth Hardy and state Rep. Jubilee McGill are expected to attend the ceremony, along with about 150 local residents and members of the Korean community. The program will also feature a rendition of “Arirang," which Hulbert transcribed into Western musical notation 130 years ago. Born in 1863, Hulbert first arrived in K

item.title: Renault Korea's sales drop 24.7% in September on weak demand
item.description: Renault Korea Motors, the Korean unit of France's Renault S.A., said Thursday its sales fell 24.7 percent in September from a year earlier amid weak demand at home. The automaker sold 6,556 vehicles last month, down from 8,710 units a year earlier, the company said in a release. Domestic sales dropped 45.2 percent on-year to 2,289 units last month, while exports backtracked 5.8 percent to 4,267 units.

item.title: GM Korea's September sales surge 73.3% on strong exports
item.description: GM Korea, the Korean unit of General Motors, said Thursday its sales surged 73.3 percent in September from a year earlier, driven by strong overseas demand. The company sold 41,101 vehicles last month, up from 23,723 units a year earlier, on robust sales of the Chevrolet Trax Crossover and the Trailblazer sport utility vehicle (SUV), GM Korea said in a press release. Domestic sales fell 40.9 percent to 727 units from 1,231, while exports jumped 79.5 percent to 40,374 from 22,492. From January to September, sales rose 17 percent to 381,785 units from 326,381 in the year-ago period. Domestic sales plunged 36.4 percent to 7,495 from 11,785 during the same period, while exports climbed 19 percent to 374,290 from 314,596. As part of its two-track strategy, GM Korea sells both locally assembled and imported vehicles in Korea, Asia's fourth-largest economy. Its current lineup consists of two locally assembled models — the Trailblazer and Trax Crossover — and one imported model, the GMC Sierra Denali. item.title: S. Korea says in communication with Ukraine over NK POW transfer disclosure
item.description: South Korea has been in diplomatic communication with Ukraine over Kyiv's unilateral disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to Seoul, the foreign ministry said Thursday. The comments came after South Korea demanded an official explanation and apology over Ukraine's disclosure of the transfer and a statement from the Ukrainian presidential office denying that there had been an agreement to keep the matter confidential. "We have conveyed our position to the Ukrainian side, and we understand that Ukraine is also reviewing it. Communication between the diplomatic authorities of the two countries is under way," a ministry official said. "Ukraine is also aware this is a sensitive matter, and given the relations between the two countries, we expect the Ukrainian side to convey its position on the matter," he added. But the official noted Ukraine has yet to issue an official response, saying it would be inappropriate to speculate on how or when it might do so. The two North Korean soldiers were captured in January 2025 while fighting for Russia in the Kursk region

item.title: Household loans fall for 1st time in six months on tightened rules, higher rates
item.description: Household loans fall for 1st time in six months on tightened rules, higher rates Household loans by major banks fell for the first time in six months last month in the face of tight borrowing regulations, data showed Thursday. Outstanding household loans at five major lenders -- KB Kookmin Bank, Shinhan Bank, Hana Bank, Woori Bank and NH Nonghyup Bank -- stood at 780.83 trillion won ($575 billion) as of end-September, down 1.28 trillion won from the previous month, according to data compiled by the banks. Household loans have been on a steady rise since April this year due to a rise in mortgage and credit loans. The fall in household loans by banks was mainly attributed to a decline in credit loans, which posted a decrease of 1.34 trillion won last month. Mortgage loans, meanwhile, continued to rise, gaining 125 billion won in September to 621.39 trillion won at the end of last month, according to the data. item.title: Korean designer helps build LEGO's first Dragon Ball set
item.description: LEGO Group has unveiled its first Dragon Ball set, created with the participation of a Korean designer at the Danish toymaker. The 1,764-piece LEGO Icons Dragon Ball Shenron & Goku set, developed in partnership with Japanese animation studio Toei Animation, will go on sale Nov. 4, the company said. Icons is LEGO's product line aimed at adult builders. Dragon Ball, created by the late Japanese manga artist Akira Toriyama, follows a boy named Goku on adventures to collect seven magical orbs known as Dragon Balls. Gathering all seven summons Shenron, a dragon that grants a wish. First published in 1984, the manga was adapted into an anime series by Toei that drew a worldwide following. The set recreates the scene in which Shenron rises from the seven Dragon Balls, with a young Goku riding his magic cloud, the Flying Nimbus. Seven bricks at the base represent the Dragon Balls, and the Goku minifigure can be detached and repositioned. A display stand and a plaque bearing the Dragon Ball logo are included. item.title: S. Korean won weakens against US dollar on lingering worries over higher yields
item.description: The South Korean won weakened against the U.S. dollar Thursday, as worries linger over the persistent rise in U.S. Treasury yields. The won was quoted at 1,358.4 won per dollar at 3:30 p.m., down 5.6 won from the close of the previous stock trading session. The won's weakness came as expectations were lowered after data showed a key U.S. inflation gauge gained less than expected in August. However, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield rose past 5.3 percent, marking the highest level in about 24 years. Foreigners sold a net 547.3 billion won ($403 million) worth of local stocks during the latest regular trading session, while the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index climbed 1.95 percent to close at 6,917.35.

item.title: Lee calls for police reform to root out cover-ups, irregularities in investigations
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung on Thursday renewed his call for thorough police reform to root out any cover-ups and other irregularities in investigations, as police are set to assume greater investigative authority under the recent revision to the Criminal Procedure Act. The president made the call during a meeting with his key aides at Cheong Wa Dae, a day before the Serious Crimes Investigation Agency (SCIA) is set to launch, along with the Public Prosecution Service, as part of the prosecution reform aimed at stripping the prosecution of investigative rights. Renamed as the Public Prosecution Service, prosecutors will only be tasked with indicting and maintaining indictments against suspects, while the SCIA will conduct investigations into corruption, defense industry crimes, insurrection and other serious crimes. Lee said the launch of the two agencies will end the era during which prosecutors wielded the authority to conduct both investigation and indictments, and acted as political prosecutors, targeting political foes and subjecting them to persecution. item.title: Hyundai Motor's Sept. sales drop 16% on fewer working days
item.description: Hyundai Motor, Korea's biggest carmaker, said Thursday its sales fell 16 percent in September from a year earlier, as there were fewer working days due to the Chuseok holiday. Hyundai sold 307,998 vehicles last month, down from 366,731 units in 2025, the company said in a press release. Domestic sales plunged 25.7 percent to 49,022 units from 66,001 a year earlier, while overseas sales declined 13.9 percent to 258,976 units from 300,730. "Fewer working days due to Chuseok and delayed demand for new models affected the monthly numbers," the carmaker said. Hyundai plans to launch the all-new Tucson sport utility vehicle (SUV) in the domestic market as it expands its SUV lineup. From January to September, cumulative sales backtracked 7 percent to 2,886,763 vehicles from 3,105,346 a year earlier. Domestic sales dropped 16.3 percent to 448,181 units in the first nine months from 535,458 a year earlier, while overseas sales declined 5.1 percent to 2,438,582 units from 2,569,888.

item.title: Korea expects faster progress in security talks with US following investment announcement
item.description: Korea expects progress in its security consultations with the United States to accelerate following the announcement of major Korean investment projects in the U.S., Seoul's foreign ministry said Thursday. U.S. President Donald Trump on Wednesday (U.S. time) announced details of Korea's planned $200 billion investment in the U.S., part of a broader $350 billion commitment agreed by the two sides last year in exchange for lower U.S. tariffs on Korean goods. The framework was outlined in a joint fact sheet issued in November following an October summit between President Lee Jae Myung and Trump, which also addressed security-related issues, including Korea's pursuit of nuclear-powered submarines and its push to secure rights for uranium enrichment and spent nuclear fuel reprocessing. item.title: Busan hot springs earns national 'spa city' status
item.description: Deep beneath the concrete and bustling avenues of Busan, Korea’s second-largest city, natural thermal waters registering a blistering 70.3 degrees Celsius have welled up through granite fissures for nearly fifteen centuries. Local folklore traces the springs back to the Silla Kingdom (57 B.C. — 936 A.D.), when an injured crane was said to have bathed in the steaming pools and flown away fully restored. The Ministry of the Interior and Safety officially recognized that heritage, Thursday, by designating the Dongnae Hot Springs District in Busan as the nation's fourth official "Spa City." The prestigious national status clears the path for municipal leaders to transform the historic bathing quarter from a traditional bathhouse hub into a modern urban wellness destination. Following field inspections and expert evaluations of Dongnae’s redevelopment strategy, federal officials selected the district based on its rare combination of high-temperature mineral waters and exceptional urban accessibility. item.title: Netflix's 'Take Charge of My Heart' recharges classic rom-com formula
item.description: An electrifying Korean romantic comedy is headed to the small screen for the fall season. Starring Kim Young-kwang and Chae Soo-bin, the Netflix series "Take Charge of My Heart" is set to spark a lovely romantic connection with viewers and warming hearts as chilly autumn days set in. The drama follows a man whose artificial heart battery is dying and a woman burdened with high-voltage superpowers. item.title: Korean firms to unveil AI service developed under gov't project: sources
item.description: Three consortia led by Korean tech companies will unveil their artificial intelligence (AI) services developed under a government-led project within this month to provide all citizens with access to AI, government and industry sources said Thursday. The three teams — led by SK Telecom, KT and Kakao, respectively — are set to launch a closed beta version of their AI services sometime in October, the sources added. The government's "AI for All" project unveiled in July came amid efforts to lower Korea's dependence on foreign AI models and boost the domestic AI sector. Developers are required to use domestic AI models for at least 50 percent of the offered AI services, with government funding and graphic processing unit (GPU) support. Developers have set a monthly active user target of 5 million for their envisioned services, with Kakao vowing to expand the figure to 10 million by 2027 and 30 million by 2030. Korea plans to inject an additional 250 billion won ($184.37 million), starting next year, to further advance the services, which include costs to secure some 2,000 GPUs. According

item.title: Han River family festival to feature films, jazz, 7,500 books
item.description: Seoul will host a family festival along the Han River from beginning Saturday, offering books, music, games and hands-on activities, the city government said Thursday. The 2026 Hangang Family Festival will be held through Oct. 18 at Gwangnaru and Jamwon Han River parks, two of the riverside parks along the Han River, which runs through the center of the capital. Gwangnaru Park will host the event every Saturday and Sunday, for a total of six days. Jamwon Park will hold a performance program by local artists, teenagers and residents on Oct. 9. Visitors can reach Jamwon Park via the Apgujeong stop of the Hangang Bus, the city's river ferry service. The festival's theme is "Hangang Moeumjip," a play on words. "Moeumjip" means an anthology, while "jip" on its own means home. The festival is meant to bring together the different interests of family members in one place. Reading areas by the water will offer about 7,500 books: 6,000 at Gwangnaru and 1,500 at Jamwon. There will be 400 seats, including beanbags, mats and shaded spots.
